title: Spanish grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Spanish, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is everyday Mexican Spanish (with ustedes for “you all”, as all of Latin America says it).

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Spanish conversation.
lessons.topic: {{soy}}, {{eres}}, {{es}} (the verb {{ser}}) and {{me llamo}}; {{tú}} and {{usted}}

goal.t: Hola, soy Ana. Soy de Chicago.
goal.tr: Hi, I'm Ana. I'm from Chicago.

dialog.t: ¡Hola! Me llamo Diego. ¿Cómo te llamas?
dialog.tr: Hi! My name is Diego. What's your name?

dialog.t: Hola, Diego. Soy Ana.
dialog.tr: Hi, Diego. I'm Ana.

dialog.t: Mucho gusto, Ana.
dialog.tr: Nice to meet you, Ana.

dialog.t: Igualmente.
dialog.tr: Likewise.

dialog.t: ¿De dónde eres?
dialog.tr: Where are you from?

dialog.t: Soy de Chicago. ¿Y tú?
dialog.tr: I'm from Chicago. And you?

dialog.t: Soy de aquí, de Guadalajara.
dialog.tr: I'm from here, from Guadalajara.

blocks.p: **Saying who you are.** {{Soy}} means “I am”: {{Soy Ana.}} “I'm Ana.” With {{de}} “from”, it says where you're from: {{Soy de Chicago.}} You can also give your name with {{Me llamo…}}, word for word “I call myself…”: {{Me llamo Ana.}} Both are everyday Spanish.

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: eat, go, live, be. {{Soy}} “I am” is a verb.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, it.

blocks.p: **Spanish usually leaves out “I”.** The pronoun for “I” is {{yo}}, but {{soy}} already means “I am”, so Spanish normally leaves {{yo}} out: {{Soy de Chicago.}} Add {{yo}} only to stress it: {{Yo soy de Chicago, ¿y tú?}} “**I**'m from Chicago, and you?”

**Two words for “you”.** Spanish has a friendly “you”, {{tú}}, for friends, family, children and people your age in relaxed places, and a polite one, {{usted}}, for people you don't know, older people, and at work. The verb changes with them:
**Asking.** A question is written between ¿ and ?: the upside-down mark warns you a question is coming. The question word comes first: {{¿De dónde eres?}} is, word for word, “from where are you?”.

ex.tr: My name is Carlos.
I'm from the United States.
I'm Laura, nice to meet you.
Are you Mr. García?
ex.note: a question just by raising your voice at the end

ex.tr: Good morning, what's your name?
ex.note: polite: to someone you don't know

blocks.tip: Hello and goodbye: {{Hola}} (hi), {{Buenos días}} (good morning), {{Buenas tardes}} (good afternoon, from about noon), {{Buenas noches}} (good evening, good night), {{Adiós}} or {{Hasta luego}} (bye). The little mark on a vowel (á, é, í, ó, ú) shows the loudest part of the word ({{adiós}}: a-DIÓS) and sometimes tells two words apart: {{tú}} “you”, {{tu}} “your”.

mistakes.why: Without {{me}}, {{llamo}} means “I call”: {{Yo llamo Ana}} sounds like “I call Ana”. Your name is {{Me llamo…}}, “I call myself…”.
To an older man you don't know, use the polite {{usted}}, and the verb goes with it: {{es usted}}, not {{eres}}.

lessons.title: Say who people are and what they do
lessons.summary: Introduce a friend and say what people do and where they're from: “She's a doctor. We're from Texas.”
lessons.topic: {{ser}} for everyone ({{soy, eres, es, somos, son}}); jobs without {{un}} or {{una}}; -o for men, -a for women

goal.t: Ella es Laura. Es doctora y es de Monterrey.
goal.tr: This is Laura. She's a doctor and she's from Monterrey.

dialog.t: Diego, ella es mi amiga Laura.
dialog.tr: Diego, this is my friend Laura.

dialog.t: Mucho gusto, Laura. ¿Eres de aquí?

dialog.tr: No, I'm from Monterrey.

blocks.p: **The verb {{ser}}.** {{Soy}} “I am” and {{eres}} “you are” are forms of one verb, {{ser}} “to be”. Here it is for everyone:

table: he is, she is, you are (polite)

blocks.p: {{Usted}} uses the same form as “he” and “she”: {{usted es}}. For more than one “you”, Mexico uses {{ustedes}} for everyone, friends and strangers alike: {{ustedes son}}. ({{Nosotras}} “we” and {{ellas}} “they” are for groups of women only.)

blocks.means: whether a word is masculine or feminine. In Spanish every word for a person or a thing has one, and the words around it change to match.

blocks.p: **Men and women.** Words for jobs and nationalities change with the person: usually **-o** for a man and **-a** for a woman: {{Él es mexicano. Ella es mexicana.}} A word ending in a consonant adds **-a** for a woman: {{doctor}} → {{doctora}}, {{profesor}} → {{profesora}}, {{inglés}} → {{inglesa}} (the accent mark goes). Words ending in **-e** or **-ista** stay the same: {{estudiante}}, {{dentista}}, {{estadounidense}} (American).

**No “a” before a job.** English says “She's **a** doctor”; Spanish says just {{Es doctora.}} The {{una}} comes back only when you describe the person: {{Es una doctora muy buena.}} “She's a very good doctor.”

ex.tr: My dad is an engineer.
We're students.
They're from Canada.
Are you Mrs. Martínez?

ex.t: Ella es enfermera y él es mesero.
ex.tr: She's a nurse and he's a waiter.
My parents are Mexican.
ex.note: {{papás}}: dad and mom together. {{Mi}} “my”, {{mis}} for more than one (lesson 10).

blocks.tip: Nationalities and languages have no capital letter in Spanish: {{Soy estadounidense}}, {{Ella es mexicana}}, {{el español}}. Countries and cities do: {{México}}, {{Canadá}}.

mistakes.why: To say what someone does, just the job, without {{una}}.
Laura is a woman: {{mexicana}}, with -a.
“We are” is {{somos}}.

lessons.title: Say how you are and where you are
lessons.summary: Ask “How are you?” and answer, and say where you are right now: the other “to be”, {{estar}}.
lessons.topic: {{estar}} ({{estoy, estás, está, estamos, están}}); {{ser}} or {{estar}}?

goal.t: Estoy bien, gracias. Estoy en la oficina.
goal.tr: I'm fine, thanks. I'm at the office.

dialog.t: ¡Hola, hijo! ¿Cómo estás?
dialog.tr: Hi, son! How are you?

dialog.t: Bien, mamá, pero un poco cansado.
dialog.tr: Fine, Mom, but a little tired.

dialog.t: ¿Dónde estás?
dialog.tr: Where are you?

dialog.t: Estoy en el trabajo. ¿Y tú, cómo estás?
dialog.tr: I'm at work. And how are you?

dialog.t: Muy bien. Tu papá y yo estamos en casa.
dialog.tr: Very well. Your dad and I are at home.

blocks.p: **A second “to be”.** Spanish has two verbs for “to be”. You've met {{ser}}: who or what someone is ({{Soy Pablo}}, {{Soy maestro}}, {{Soy de Texas}}). The other one, {{estar}}, says **how** someone is right now and **where** someone or something is:

table: he is, she is, you are (polite)
you are (all of you), they are

blocks.p: Mind the accent marks: {{estás}}, {{está}}, {{están}} are said es-TÁS, es-TÁ, es-TÁN, loudest at the end.
**{{ser}} or {{estar}}?** A first rule that works most of the time: **{{ser}} for what someone or something is** (name, job, where they're from), **{{estar}} for how they are and where they are**.

table: {{Está en la escuela.}} She's at school.

ex.tr: How are you, ma'am?
I'm very happy.
ex.note: said by a woman; a man says {{contento}}

ex.tr: My brother is sick.
Where are my keys?
We're downtown.

ex.t: El baño está a la derecha.
ex.tr: The bathroom is on the right.

blocks.p: Words for how you feel change for men and women, like jobs: {{cansado}} / {{cansada}} (tired), {{contento}} / {{contenta}} (happy), {{enfermo}} / {{enferma}} (sick), {{ocupado}} / {{ocupada}} (busy). {{Bien}} (well, fine) and {{mal}} (bad, not well) never change.

blocks.tip: {{¿Cómo estás?}} asks how you are; {{¿Cómo eres?}}, with {{ser}}, asks what you're like as a person. Answer {{¿Cómo estás?}} with {{Bien, gracias}}, {{Más o menos}} (so-so) or {{Muy bien, ¿y tú?}}

Where someone is: {{estar}}.

lessons.title: Name things: a, the and more than one
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?” and name things, one or many: {{el libro}}, {{la mesa}}, {{unos tacos}}.
lessons.topic: nouns and their gender; {{el, la, los, las}} and {{un, una, unos, unas}}; plurals

goal.t: ¿Qué es esto? — Es un tamal.
goal.tr: What's this? — It's a tamal.

dialog.t: Disculpe, ¿qué es esto?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, what's this?

dialog.t: Es un tamal de rajas.
dialog.tr: It's a tamal with poblano peppers.

dialog.t: ¿Y eso?
dialog.tr: And that?

dialog.t: Es una gordita. Y aquí están los tamales de pollo.
dialog.tr: It's a gordita. And here are the chicken tamales.

dialog.t: Un tamal de pollo, por favor.
dialog.tr: A chicken tamal, please.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a place or a thing: friend, city, book, coffee.

blocks.p: **Every noun has a gender.** In Spanish not only people but things are masculine or feminine. There's no meaning to look for ({{libro}} “book” is masculine, {{mesa}} “table” is feminine), but the ending usually tells you: most nouns in **-o** are masculine, most in **-a** are feminine.

blocks.means: a little word before a noun: “the”, “a”.

blocks.p: **“The” and “a”** change with the gender, and with the number:

**More than one.** A noun ending in a vowel adds **-s**: {{taco}} → {{tacos}}. One ending in a consonant adds **-es**: {{ciudad}} → {{ciudades}} (city), {{flor}} → {{flores}} (flower). A final **-z** becomes **-ces**: {{lápiz}} → {{lápices}} (pencil).

**Learn each noun with its article.** A few break the -o/-a rule: {{el día}} (the day), {{el mapa}}, {{el problema}}, but {{la mano}} (the hand), {{la foto}}. Nouns ending in **-ción** and **-dad** are feminine: {{la canción}} (the song), {{la ciudad}}. Others you simply learn: {{el café}}, {{la calle}} (the street), {{el hotel}}, {{la noche}} (the night).

ex.tr: What's that? — It's a pen.
ex.note: in Mexico a pen is a {{pluma}}

{{mesa}} is feminine: {{una}}.

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say what people and things are like, and how they are today: “a big city”, “the soup is cold”.
lessons.topic: adjectives after the noun, matching it; {{muy}}; {{es}} or {{está}} with an adjective

goal.t: Mi ciudad es grande y muy bonita.
goal.tr: My city is big and very pretty.

dialog.t: ¿Qué tal los tacos?
dialog.tr: How are the tacos?

dialog.t: ¡Están muy ricos! ¿Y tu sopa?
dialog.tr: They're really good! And your soup?

dialog.t: Está un poco fría.
dialog.tr: It's a little cold.

dialog.t: Es un restaurante muy bueno, pero el mesero está muy ocupado.
dialog.tr: It's a very good restaurant, but the waiter is very busy.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, red, tired, Mexican.

blocks.p: **After the noun.** In Spanish the adjective usually comes after the noun, the other way round from English: {{una ciudad grande}} “a big city”, {{un carro rojo}} “a red car”, {{el vino blanco}} “the white wine”.

blocks.means: to change so as to match another word. A Spanish adjective agrees with its noun: it takes the noun's gender and number.

blocks.p: **It agrees with its noun**, in gender and in number:

Adjectives ending in **-e** or in a consonant have no feminine form, only a plural: {{un parque grande}}, {{una ciudad grande}}, {{dos ciudades grandes}}; {{un examen difícil}}, {{dos exámenes difíciles}}. {{Muy}} “very” goes before the adjective and never changes: {{muy bonita}}, {{muy grandes}}.
**{{es}} or {{está}}?** With adjectives, {{ser}} says what someone or something is like, {{estar}} how they are now, or how they seem to you right now:

table: {{La sopa de aquí es muy buena.}} The soup here is very good.
{{La sopa está fría.}} The soup is cold.
{{Mi hermana es muy seria.}} My sister is a serious person.
{{Mi hermana está muy seria hoy.}} My sister is very serious today.

ex.tr: It's a very nice hotel.
The streets are very quiet.
The coffee is very hot.
My grandmother is really nice.
The tacos are delicious!
The question is difficult.

blocks.tip: A few common adjectives can go before the noun, and then get shorter: {{bueno}} → {{un buen restaurante}} (a good restaurant), {{malo}} → {{un mal día}} (a bad day), {{grande}} → {{una gran ciudad}} (before the noun it means “great”, not “big”).

mistakes.why: The adjective goes after the noun.
The adjective agrees: {{casas}} is feminine and plural, so {{bonitas}}.
The soup is cold now, not cold by nature: {{está}}.

lessons.title: Order food and drinks
lessons.summary: Order at a café or a taco stand, and say what you want to do: “I'd like two tacos and a coffee, please.”
lessons.topic: {{quiero}} + a noun; {{quiero}} + an infinitive; {{¿Me da…?}} and {{¿Me trae…?}}

goal.t: Quiero dos tacos y un café, por favor.
goal.tr: I'd like two tacos and a coffee, please.

dialog.t: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué les traigo?
dialog.tr: Good afternoon. What can I get you?

dialog.t: Para mí, un café con leche, por favor.
dialog.tr: A coffee with milk for me, please.

dialog.t: Yo quiero un jugo de naranja.
dialog.tr: I'd like an orange juice.

dialog.t: ¿Algo de comer?
dialog.tr: Anything to eat?

dialog.tr: Yes, we'd like two molletes (bean and cheese rolls).

dialog.t: Muy bien. Ahorita se los traigo.
dialog.tr: Very good. I'll bring them right away.

blocks.p: **Wanting a thing.** {{Quiero}} “I want”, then the thing: {{Quiero un café.}} With {{por favor}} it isn't rude at all: it's the normal way to order. In shops and at stands, Mexicans very often ask {{¿Me da…?}} “Will you give me…?”: {{¿Me da un refresco, por favor?}} And {{Para mí, …}} is “For me, …”: {{Para mí, una limonada.}}

table: he wants, she wants, you want (polite)

blocks.p: Look at the forms: {{quiero}}, {{quieres}}, {{quiere}}, {{quieren}} have **ie**, but {{queremos}} keeps the **e** of {{querer}}. Lesson 19 shows that many verbs do this.

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: to eat, to go. Spanish infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir: {{hablar}}, {{comer}}, {{vivir}}.

blocks.p: **Wanting to do something.** After {{quiero}}, the second verb is an infinitive, like English “to …”: {{Quiero comer.}} “I want to eat.” {{Quiero pagar.}} “I want to pay.” There's no word for “to”: the -ar, -er, -ir ending already says it.

ex.t: Quiero una mesa para dos, por favor.
ex.tr: I'd like a table for two, please.
What do you want to drink?
ex.note: {{tomar}} “to take” is also the everyday word for “to drink”

ex.tr: We'd like to order, please.
Can I have a kilo of tortillas?
ex.note: word for word “Do you give me…?”: the usual way to ask in a shop

ex.tr: Can I have the check, please?
ex.note: {{¿Me trae…?}} “Will you bring me…?”, at a table

ex.tr: I don't want coffee, thanks.
My son wants some quesadillas.

blocks.tip: {{Con}} is “with” and {{sin}} “without”: {{un café sin azúcar}}, {{tacos sin cebolla}}, {{un té con limón}}.

mistakes.why: No word for “to”: the infinitive comes right after {{quiero}}.
“I want” is {{quiero}}, with -o. {{Quiere}} is “he wants”, “she wants”.

lessons.title: Say what you do every day
lessons.summary: Talk about your work, your studies and your day: “I work at a hospital and I study English at night.”
lessons.topic: the present of -ar verbs ({{hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan}}); {{no}} before the verb

goal.t: Trabajo en un hospital y estudio inglés en la noche.
goal.tr: I work at a hospital and I study English at night.

dialog.t: ¿Trabajas o estudias?
dialog.tr: Do you work or study?

dialog.t: Trabajo. Soy enfermera y trabajo en un hospital.
dialog.tr: I work. I'm a nurse, and I work at a hospital.

dialog.t: ¿Y hablas español en el trabajo?
dialog.tr: And do you speak Spanish at work?

dialog.t: Sí, mucho. Muchos pacientes hablan español.
dialog.tr: Yes, a lot. Lots of patients speak Spanish.

dialog.t: ¡Qué bien! Yo trabajo en una oficina y estudio en la noche.
dialog.tr: Great! I work at an office and study at night.

blocks.p: **Verbs change for each person.** In English, “work” hardly changes: I work, she work**s**. In Spanish the ending changes for every person, and the ending tells you who is doing it. Take the infinitive {{hablar}} “to speak”, drop **-ar**, and add the endings:

blocks.means: to change a verb's ending to show who is doing it: {{hablar}} → {{hablo}} “I speak”, {{hablas}} “you speak”.

blocks.p: Most -ar verbs work exactly like this: {{estudiar}} (to study), {{cocinar}} (to cook), {{escuchar}} (to listen), {{llegar}} (to arrive), {{tomar}} (to take, to drink), {{manejar}} (to drive), {{caminar}} (to walk), {{necesitar}} (to need), {{comprar}} (to buy). One Spanish present covers English “I work”, “I'm working” and “I do work”.

**Who?** Since the ending says who, Spanish usually leaves out {{yo}}, {{tú}} and {{nosotros}}: {{Trabajo en una oficina.}} “He”, “she” and polite “you” share one form, so say the person when it isn't clear: {{Ella trabaja aquí.}} {{¿Usted habla inglés?}}
**Not.** Put {{no}} right before the verb: {{No hablo francés.}} “I don't speak French.” Spanish needs no extra word like “don't”.

ex.tr: I speak a little Spanish.
My husband cooks really well.
Where do you work?
We study at the same school.
My kids don't drink coffee.
I need a taxi.
You all work a lot.

blocks.tip: In a question the ending does all the work: {{¿Hablas inglés?}} is just {{Hablas inglés}} with a question in your voice. Spanish has no “do” for questions.

mistakes.why: With {{yo}}, the ending is -o: {{trabajo}}.
{{No}} goes right before the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Yo estoy trabajo en un hospital.
mistakes.why: One verb is enough: {{trabajo}} already means “I work”.

practice.tr: My parents work in a store.

lessons.topic: the present of -er and -ir verbs ({{como, comes, come…}}, {{vivo, vives, vive…}})

goal.t: Vivo en Guadalajara y como en casa con mi familia.
goal.tr: I live in Guadalajara and I eat at home with my family.

blocks.p: **Two more groups.** Spanish infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir. You know the -ar endings. Verbs in **-er** and **-ir** use **e** where -ar verbs use **a**, and the two groups are the same except for “we”:

**-er verbs** like {{comer}}: {{beber}} (to drink), {{leer}} (to read), {{aprender}} (to learn), {{vender}} (to sell), {{correr}} (to run), {{creer}} (to believe, to think). **-ir verbs** like {{vivir}}: {{escribir}} (to write), {{abrir}} (to open), {{recibir}} (to receive), {{subir}} (to go up), {{compartir}} (to share).
**The trick:** for “I”, all three groups end in **-o** ({{hablo}}, {{como}}, {{vivo}}). Only “we” shows the infinitive's own vowel: {{hablamos}}, {{comemos}}, {{vivimos}}.

{{No}} goes right before the verb.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask for information: what, who, where, when, how, how much and why.
lessons.topic: yes/no questions; {{qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, por qué, cuál}}

goal.t: ¿Qué estudias y por qué?
goal.tr: What are you studying, and why?

blocks.p: **Yes or no.** The simplest question is an ordinary sentence with your voice going up at the end: {{Hablas inglés.}} “You speak English.” → {{¿Hablas inglés?}} “Do you speak English?” Spanish needs no “do”. In writing, a question opens with ¿ and closes with ?.
**Question words** come first, and they always carry an accent mark:
**Why and because.** {{¿Por qué?}}, two words with an accent, asks “why?”; {{porque}}, one word with no accent, answers “because”: {{¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque vivo en México.}}
**After the question word** comes the verb, and then the person, if you name one: {{¿Dónde trabaja tu hermano?}} “Where does your brother work?”, word for word “where works your brother?”.

**Little words go first.** A word like {{de}} “from” or {{con}} “with” goes before the question word, never at the end as in English: {{¿De dónde eres?}} “Where are you from?” {{¿Con quién vives?}} “Who do you live with?”

lessons.summary: Say who's in your family, how old people are, and whose things are whose: {{tengo}}, {{mi}}, {{tu}}, {{su}}.
lessons.topic: {{tener}} ({{tengo, tienes, tiene…}}); {{mi, tu, su, nuestro}}; {{tener … años}} for age

goal.t: Tengo un hermano y una hermana. Mi hermana tiene veinte años.

blocks.p: **{{tener}} “to have”** is one of the most used verbs in Spanish, and it's irregular: learn it by heart.

table: he has, she has, you have (polite)

blocks.p: **Age is something you have.** Spanish says how many years you **have**: {{Tengo treinta años.}} “I'm thirty”, word for word “I have thirty years”. Ask with {{¿Cuántos años tienes?}} “How old are you?”

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, our.

blocks.p: **my, your, his…** go before the noun. They match the number of the things owned (one or more), not the owner; {{nuestro}} “our” also matches their gender:

{{su}} can be his, her, their or polite “your”: the situation makes it clear. When it doesn't, use {{de}} and the person: {{la casa de Ana}} “Ana's house”. Spanish has no 's: it says “the house of Ana”.

**Family words**: {{papá}}, {{mamá}}, {{papás}} (parents), {{hermano}} / {{hermana}}, {{hijo}} / {{hija}}, {{esposo}} / {{esposa}}, {{abuelo}} / {{abuela}}, {{tío}} / {{tía}}, {{primo}} / {{prima}} (cousin), {{sobrino}} / {{sobrina}} (nephew, niece). A masculine plural covers a mixed group: {{mis hermanos}} can be brothers and sisters, {{mis hijos}} sons and daughters.

ex.tr: I have three children.
My mom is sixty.
How old is your son?
Our house is small.

ex.t: Ella es la esposa de mi hermano.
ex.tr: She's my brother's wife.

blocks.tip: Numbers for ages: {{veinte}} (20), {{treinta}} (30), {{cuarenta}} (40), {{cincuenta}} (50), {{sesenta}} (60), {{setenta}} (70), {{ochenta}} (80). In between, with {{y}}: {{treinta y cinco}} (35). From 16 to 29 they are one word: {{dieciocho}} (18), {{veinticinco}} (25).

lessons.summary: Say what you like and don't like, and ask others: “I really like tacos, but I don't like very spicy food.”
lessons.topic: {{me gusta}} and {{me gustan}}; {{te, le, nos, les}}; {{a mí también}}, {{a mí tampoco}}

goal.t: Me gustan mucho los tacos, pero no me gusta la comida muy picante.
goal.tr: I really like tacos, but I don't like very spicy food.

blocks.means: who or what does the verb: in “Ana works”, it's Ana. In Spanish the verb's ending matches its subject.

blocks.p: **Back to front.** Spanish doesn't say “I like coffee”. It says {{Me gusta el café}}: “coffee pleases me”. The thing you like is the subject, the verb {{gusta}} goes with it, and {{me}} “to me” says who likes it.
**One thing or more?** The verb matches the thing you like: {{gusta}} for one thing, or for doing something; {{gustan}} for more than one thing:
**Who likes it?** Change the little word in front:

table: he likes, she likes, you like (polite)

blocks.p: Spanish keeps “the” even for things in general: {{Me gusta el café}}, {{Me gustan los perros}} “I like dogs”.

**Me too, me neither.** Answer with {{a}} and the person: {{A mí también.}} “Me too.” {{A mí tampoco.}} “Me neither” (after a “not”). {{A mí sí.}} / {{A mí no.}} when you feel differently. {{¿Y a ti?}} turns it back: “And you?”. The same {{a}} names who: {{A mi papá le gusta el futbol.}} “My dad likes soccer.”

blocks.tip: {{Mucho}} goes after {{gusta}}: {{Me gusta mucho.}} “I like it a lot.” And {{¿Te gusta?}} with nothing after it means “Do you like it?”: no word for “it” is needed.

mistakes.why: {{gustar}} works back to front: “coffee pleases me”, {{me gusta}}.
More than one thing: {{gustan}}.
Spanish keeps the article when you talk about something in general.

goal.t: ¿Cuánto cuesta esta playera? — Doscientos pesos.
goal.tr: How much is this T-shirt? — Two hundred pesos.

dialog.t: Buenas tardes. ¿Cuánto cuesta este sombrero?

dialog.t: Ándele, pues. Doscientos.
dialog.tr: Okay then. Two hundred.

blocks.means: a word that points: this, that, these, those.

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{este}} is “this” (near me), {{ese}} is “that” (near you, or a little way off). Like adjectives, they match the noun:

They also stand alone for “this one”, “that one”: {{Quiero ese.}} “I want that one.” For something you can't name, or an idea, use {{esto}} and {{eso}}, which never change: {{¿Qué es esto?}} {{Eso es.}} “That's it.” For something far from both of you there's {{aquel}} “that … over there” ({{aquella casa}}), but in everyday Mexican Spanish {{ese}} usually does the job.
**How much?** The verb {{costar}} “to cost” matches the thing: {{¿Cuánto cuesta?}} for one, {{¿Cuánto cuestan?}} for more than one. The answer: {{Cuesta cien pesos.}} {{Cuestan cincuenta.}}

Build bigger numbers piece by piece, with {{y}} only between the tens and the ones: {{treinta y cinco}} (35), {{ciento treinta y cinco}} (135), {{mil doscientos}} (1,200). {{cien}} is exactly 100; above it, {{ciento}}.

I want that one, the red one.

ex.t: ¿Me da un kilo de esas naranjas?
ex.tr: Can I have a kilo of those oranges?
That's five hundred forty pesos.
Do you take cards?

blocks.tip: At markets, prices are often said without {{pesos}}: {{Son ochenta.}} “That's eighty.” {{¿Me hace un descuento?}} “Can you give me a discount?” is worth knowing too.

{{playera}} is feminine: {{esta}}.

lessons.summary: Find a pharmacy, an ATM or the bathroom: “Is there a pharmacy around here?”, and understand the answer.
lessons.topic: {{hay}} (there is, there are) or {{está}} (where it is); {{cerca de, al lado de, enfrente de}}; {{de}} + {{el}} = {{del}}

goal.t: Disculpe, ¿hay una farmacia por aquí?
goal.tr: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy around here?

dialog.t: Disculpe, ¿hay una farmacia por aquí?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy around here?

dialog.t: Sí, hay una en la esquina, al lado del banco.
dialog.tr: Yes, there's one on the corner, next to the bank.

blocks.p: **{{hay}}: there is, there are.** One little word for both, and it never changes: {{Hay un banco.}} “There's a bank.” {{Hay dos bancos.}} “There are two banks.” {{¿Hay…?}} asks “Is there…?” or “Are there…?”, and {{No hay…}} says “There isn't…”, “There aren't…”.

**{{hay}} or {{está}}?** {{hay}} says that something exists somewhere, usually with {{un}}, {{una}}, a number, or nothing before the noun. {{está}} (more than one: {{están}}) says **where** a particular thing is: one with {{el}}, {{la}}, a name, or {{mi}}, {{tu}}…

table: {{¿Hay un baño por aquí?}} Is there a bathroom around here?
{{¿Dónde está el baño?}} Where's the bathroom?
{{Hay una farmacia en la esquina.}} There's a pharmacy on the corner.
{{La farmacia está en la esquina.}} The pharmacy is on the corner.
{{La leche está en el refri.}} The milk is in the fridge.

blocks.means: a little word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, often to say where or when: in, on, next to, from.

blocks.p: **Where things are.** Many of these end in {{de}}: {{cerca de}} (near), {{lejos de}} (far from), {{al lado de}} (next to), {{enfrente de}} (across from, in front of), {{detrás de}} (behind), {{a la derecha de}} and {{a la izquierda de}} (to the right, to the left of). Others: {{en}} (in, on, at), {{entre}} (between), {{en la esquina}} (on the corner).

**{{de}} + {{el}} = {{del}}.** When {{de}} meets {{el}}, the two join: {{al lado del banco}} “next to the bank”. With {{la}}, {{los}} and {{las}} nothing joins: {{al lado de la iglesia}} “next to the church”.

ex.tr: Is there an ATM around here?

ex.t: El hotel está enfrente del parque.

ex.t: Hay muchos restaurantes en el centro.
ex.tr: There are lots of restaurants downtown.

ex.t: Mi casa está cerca de la escuela.
ex.tr: My house is near the school.
There's no parking.
ex.note: {{no hay}} + a noun with no article: “there's no…”

ex.t: Los baños están al fondo, a la derecha.
ex.tr: The restrooms are at the back, on the right.

blocks.tip: {{por aquí}} “around here” makes a question gentler: {{¿Hay un Oxxo por aquí?}} (Oxxo: the convenience store on every Mexican corner). Start with {{Disculpe}} “Excuse me”, and thank with {{Muchas gracias}}; the answer is {{De nada}}.

lessons.summary: Say where you're going and how you get there: “I'm going downtown by subway.”
lessons.topic: {{ir}} “to go” ({{voy, vas, va, vamos, van}}); {{a}} + {{el}} = {{al}}; {{en camión}}, {{a pie}}

goal.t: Voy al centro en metro.
goal.tr: I'm going downtown by subway.

dialog.t: ¡Buenos días! ¿Adónde vas tan temprano?
dialog.tr: Good morning! Where are you going so early?

blocks.p: **{{ir}} “to go”** is irregular, but its endings look like the -ar ones you know:

table: he goes, she goes, you go (polite)

blocks.p: **Where to: {{a}}.** After {{ir}}, the place comes with {{a}} “to”: {{Voy a México.}} {{Vamos a la playa.}} When {{a}} meets {{el}}, they join into {{al}}: {{Voy al mercado}}, {{Va al banco}}. (Only {{el}} joins: {{a la}}, {{a los}}, {{a las}} stay apart.) To ask: {{¿Adónde vas?}} or {{¿A dónde vas?}} “Where are you going?”

**How: {{en}}.** {{en carro}} (by car), {{en camión}} (by bus: in Mexico a city bus is a {{camión}}), {{en metro}}, {{en taxi}}, {{en avión}} (by plane), {{en bici}}. But on foot is {{a pie}}, or simply {{caminando}}.
The present of {{ir}} is both “I go” and “I'm going”: {{Voy al gimnasio los lunes}} “I go to the gym on Mondays”, {{Voy al súper}} “I'm going to the supermarket”.

ex.tr: Where are you all going?
We're going to the movies on Saturday.

Coming!

On foot is {{a pie}}; vehicles take {{en}}: {{en carro}}, {{en camión}}.

lessons.title: Say what time and what day
lessons.summary: Ask and tell the time, and say when things happen: “The class is on Tuesday at six in the evening.”
lessons.topic: {{¿Qué hora es?}}; {{es la una}}, {{son las…}}; {{a las…}}; {{el lunes}}, {{los lunes}}; {{ser}} for when and where an event is

goal.t: La clase es el martes a las seis de la tarde.
goal.tr: The class is on Tuesday at six in the evening.

dialog.t: Consultorio del doctor Ruiz, buenos días.
dialog.tr: Dr. Ruiz's office, good morning.

dialog.t: Buenos días. ¿Hay citas para el jueves?

dialog.t: Perfecto. Su cita es el jueves a las diez y media.

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{¿Qué hora es?}} The answer is {{Son las}} + the number, because hours are plural ({{las}} stands for {{las horas}}): {{Son las tres.}} “It's three.” Only one o'clock is singular: {{Es la una.}}

**At what time?** {{a las}} + the hour: {{a las ocho}} “at eight”, {{a la una}} “at one”. {{¿A qué hora…?}} asks “What time…?”. Add the part of the day: {{de la mañana}} (in the morning), {{de la tarde}} (in the afternoon, early evening), {{de la noche}} (at night).

**Days.** {{lunes}}, {{martes}}, {{miércoles}}, {{jueves}}, {{viernes}}, {{sábado}}, {{domingo}}, with no capital letter. “On Monday” is {{el lunes}}, with no word for “on”; “on Mondays”, every week, is {{los lunes}}.

**When and where an event is: {{ser}}.** You know {{estar}} for where things are. But for an event (a class, a party, a meeting), Spanish uses {{ser}}, for its time and also for its place: {{La fiesta es el sábado.}} {{La fiesta es en mi casa.}} “The party is at my house.”

ex.tr: What time does the bank open?
I work from nine to five.

ex.t: Los sábados como con mis papás.
ex.tr: On Saturdays I have lunch with my parents.
ex.note: {{comer}} is also the big midday meal

ex.t: La reunión es a las once.
ex.tr: The meeting is at eleven.

ex.t: Llego a casa a las siete de la noche.
ex.tr: I get home at seven in the evening.

ex.t: La boda es en una iglesia muy bonita.
ex.tr: The wedding is in a very beautiful church.

ex.t: ¿Qué día es hoy? — Hoy es viernes.
ex.tr: What day is it today? — Today is Friday.

blocks.tip: {{Nos vemos a las ocho.}} “See you at eight.” With {{como}}, a time is approximate: {{como a las ocho}} “around eight”.

lessons.title: Make plans
lessons.summary: Say what you're going to do and suggest plans: “This weekend I'm going to visit my parents.”
lessons.topic: {{ir a}} + infinitive, the everyday future; {{vamos a}} + infinitive for “let's”; words for when

goal.t: Este fin de semana voy a visitar a mis papás.
goal.tr: This weekend I'm going to visit my parents.

dialog.t: ¿Qué vas a hacer mañana?
dialog.tr: What are you going to do tomorrow?

dialog.t: Voy a limpiar la casa. ¿Y tú?
dialog.tr: I'm going to clean the house. And you?

dialog.t: Voy a ver el partido con mis primos. ¿Quieres venir?
dialog.tr: I'm going to watch the game with my cousins. Do you want to come?

dialog.t: ¡Sí! ¿A qué hora?

dialog.t: A las cinco. Vamos a hacer carne asada.
dialog.tr: At five. We're going to have a cookout.

blocks.p: **The future with {{ir}}.** You know {{Voy al mercado}} “I'm going to the market”. Put {{a}} and an infinitive after {{ir}}, and you have the future that Mexicans use every day: {{ir a}} + infinitive, just like English “going to”:
Only {{ir}} changes; the second verb stays an infinitive. {{No}} goes before {{ir}}: {{No voy a ir.}} “I'm not going to go.”
**Let's.** {{Vamos a}} + infinitive is also “let's…”: {{¡Vamos a comer!}} “Let's eat!” Your voice and the situation say which you mean.

**When?** {{hoy}} (today), {{mañana}} (tomorrow), {{pasado mañana}} (the day after tomorrow), {{esta noche}} (tonight), {{este fin de semana}} (this weekend), {{la próxima semana}} or {{la semana que viene}} (next week), {{el próximo año}} (next year). They go at the start or the end: {{Mañana voy a trabajar}} or {{Voy a trabajar mañana}}.

ex.tr: It's going to rain tomorrow.
What are you all going to do on vacation?

ex.t: Vamos a comprar un carro nuevo.
ex.tr: We're going to buy a new car.

ex.t: Esta noche no voy a salir.
ex.tr: I'm not going out tonight.

ex.t: Mi hermana va a tener un bebé.
ex.tr: My sister is going to have a baby.
Let's dance!

blocks.tip: **The personal a.** The goal sentence has a second {{a}}: {{visitar a mis papás}}. Spanish puts {{a}} before a person who receives the action: {{Voy a ver a mi abuela}} “I'm going to see my grandmother”, but {{Voy a ver una película}} “I'm going to see a movie”. Lesson 24 comes back to it.

mistakes.why: Don't forget the {{a}}: {{ir a}} + infinitive.
After {{ir a}}, the infinitive: {{comer}}.

mistakes.right: Voy a visitar a mis papás.
mistakes.tr: I'm going to visit my parents.
mistakes.why: Before a person who receives the action, Spanish puts {{a}}.

lessons.title: Say what you can and have to do
lessons.summary: Say what you can, can't and have to do, and ask for permission or a favor: “I can't go out today: I have to work.”
lessons.topic: {{poder}} + infinitive; {{¿Puedo…?}}, {{¿Me puede…?}}; {{tener que}} + infinitive; {{hay que}} + infinitive

goal.t: Hoy no puedo salir: tengo que trabajar.
goal.tr: I can't go out today: I have to work.

dialog.t: ¿Puedes venir a mi casa hoy?
dialog.tr: Can you come over today?

dialog.t: Hoy no puedo. Tengo que terminar un proyecto.
dialog.tr: I can't today. I have to finish a project.

dialog.t: ¿Y mañana?
dialog.tr: And tomorrow?

dialog.t: Mañana sí puedo. ¿Puedo llevar a mi novio?
dialog.tr: Tomorrow I can. Can I bring my boyfriend?

dialog.t: ¡Claro! Pero hay que llegar temprano, porque vamos a cenar a las ocho.
dialog.tr: Of course! But you have to come early, because we're having dinner at eight.

blocks.p: **Can: {{poder}}.** Like {{querer}}, it changes its vowel, here **o → ue**, except for “we”. And like {{querer}}, an infinitive comes right after it:

**Asking.** {{¿Puedo…?}} asks for permission: {{¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?}} “Can I pay by card?” {{¿Puedes…?}} or {{¿Puede…?}} asks for a favor, with {{me}} “me” before the verb: {{¿Me puede ayudar?}} “Can you help me?”
**Have to: {{tener que}}.** {{tener}} + {{que}} + infinitive: {{Tengo que trabajar.}} “I have to work.” {{Mi hijo tiene que estudiar.}} “My son has to study.”
**{{hay que}}: you have to**, for everyone, without saying who: {{Hay que pagar en la caja.}} “You have to pay at the register.” Here {{hay}} never changes.

ex.tr: May I come in?

ex.t: No podemos ir a la boda.
ex.tr: We can't go to the wedding.
Could you give me the address?
I have to go to the doctor.

ex.t: Tenemos que salir a las siete.
ex.tr: We have to leave at seven.
You need to book ahead.
You don't have to pay anything.

blocks.tip: {{poder}} is “can” in the sense of being able, or allowed. For a skill you've learned, Spanish uses {{saber}} “to know how”: {{Sé nadar}} “I can swim” (lesson 24).

mistakes.why: {{poder}} changes o → ue: {{puedo}}.
“Have to” needs {{que}}: {{tener que}} + infinitive.
The infinitive comes right after {{puedo}}, with no {{a}}.

goal.t: Los sábados salgo con mis amigos y los domingos no hago nada.

blocks.p: **“I” ends in -go.** A handful of very common verbs are regular except for one form, “I”, which ends in **-go**. The other forms follow the patterns you know:

blocks.means: a verb that doesn't follow the usual pattern in some of its forms, like {{ser}}, {{ir}} and {{tener}}. The most used verbs are often irregular.

blocks.p: Two more have the **-go** and also change their vowel in some forms:

**{{hacer}}** is both “do” and “make”: {{¿Qué haces?}} “What are you doing?” or “What do you do?”, {{Hago la comida}} “I make lunch”. When the answer is “nothing”, Spanish keeps {{no}} as well: {{No hago nada.}} “I don't do anything” (lesson 22).
**{{salir}}** is “to go out” or “to leave”: {{Salgo con mis amigos}} “I go out with my friends”, {{Salgo de casa a las siete}} “I leave home at seven” (leaving a place: {{salir de}}).

ex.tr: What are you doing this weekend?

ex.t: Salgo del trabajo a las seis.
ex.tr: I get off work at six.
Are you coming to the party?

ex.t: Siempre traigo mi comida al trabajo.
ex.tr: I always bring my lunch to work.
Where do I put the bags?

ex.t: Mi mamá dice que la comida está lista.
ex.tr: My mom says the food is ready.

ex.t: Los viernes vemos películas en casa.
ex.tr: On Fridays we watch movies at home.

blocks.tip: Two other verbs are irregular only for “I”: {{ver}} → {{veo}} (I see, I watch) and {{saber}} → {{sé}} (I know). Among friends, {{¿Qué haces?}} is the natural “What are you up to?”.

“I” of {{salir}} is {{salgo}}.
{{venir}} changes e → ie: {{vienes}}.

lessons.summary: Say what you prefer, what you order and when things start: “I prefer tea, but my husband always orders coffee.”
lessons.topic: stem-changing verbs: e → ie ({{prefiero}}), o → ue ({{duermo}}), u → ue ({{juego}}), e → i ({{pido}})

goal.t: Prefiero el té, pero mi esposo siempre pide café.
goal.tr: I prefer tea, but my husband always orders coffee.

dialog.t: ¿Quieres ver una película o prefieres jugar dominó?
dialog.tr: Do you want to watch a movie, or would you rather play dominoes?

dialog.t: Prefiero ver una película. ¿A qué hora empieza?

dialog.tr: Oh, that's a little late. I don't sleep much on weeknights.

blocks.means: a verb whose stem (the part before -ar, -er or -ir) changes its vowel in most forms: {{querer}} → {{quiero}}, {{poder}} → {{puedo}}.

blocks.p: **Verbs that change their vowel.** You've met {{quiero}} (from {{querer}}) and {{puedo}} (from {{poder}}). Many verbs do this: the last vowel of the stem changes in every form **except “we”** ({{queremos}}, {{podemos}}). Draw a line around the forms that change and it looks like a boot, so teachers call them “boot verbs”.

The infinitive doesn't warn you, so learn the common ones in their groups. **e → ie**: {{querer}}, {{preferir}}, {{pensar}} (to think), {{empezar}} (to start), {{entender}} (to understand), {{cerrar}} (to close), {{sentir}} (to feel). **o → ue**: {{poder}}, {{dormir}}, {{volver}} (to come back), {{costar}} (to cost), {{encontrar}} (to find), {{almorzar}} (to have lunch). **e → i**: {{pedir}} (to ask for, to order), {{servir}} (to serve), {{repetir}} (to repeat). And one on its own, **u → ue**: {{jugar}} (to play): {{juego}}, {{juegas}}, {{juega}}, {{jugamos}}, {{juegan}}.
{{tener}} ({{tienes}}, {{tiene}}) and {{venir}} ({{vienes}}) are boot verbs too, besides their -go for “I”.

ex.tr: What time does the movie start?
I don't understand. Could you repeat that, please?
On Sundays we play soccer.
ex.note: Mexicans say and write {{futbol}}, stressed at the end

mistakes.why: {{preferir}} changes e → ie: {{prefiero}}.
“We” never changes its vowel: {{queremos}}, {{podemos}}, {{dormimos}}.
Asking for something is {{pedir}}; {{preguntar}} is asking a question.

lessons.title: Describe your daily routine
lessons.summary: Tell someone about your day, from getting up to going to bed: “I get up at six, take a shower and head to work.”
lessons.topic: reflexive verbs ({{me levanto, te bañas, se viste…}}); where {{me, te, se}} go

goal.t: Me levanto a las seis, me baño y me voy al trabajo.
goal.tr: I get up at six, take a shower and head to work.

dialog.t: ¿A qué hora te levantas?
dialog.tr: What time do you get up?

dialog.t: Me levanto a las seis y media. ¿Por qué?
dialog.tr: I get up at six thirty. Why?

dialog.t: Porque yo me baño a las siete. ¿Tú te bañas en la mañana o en la noche?

dialog.t: En la noche. En la mañana solo me lavo la cara y me visto.

dialog.t: ¡Perfecto!

blocks.means: a verb used with {{me, te, se, nos}} because the action falls back on the person who does it: {{me baño}} “I bathe (myself)”.

blocks.p: **Doing something to yourself.** Many everyday actions in Spanish take a little pronoun that points back to the person: {{me}}, {{te}}, {{se}}… {{Me baño}} is, word for word, “I bathe myself”; {{Me levanto}} “I raise myself”: I get up.

In the dictionary these verbs end in **-se**: {{levantarse}}, {{bañarse}} (to shower, to take a bath), {{despertarse}} (to wake up: e → ie), {{vestirse}} (to get dressed: e → i), {{lavarse}} (to wash), {{peinarse}} (to do your hair), {{acostarse}} (to go to bed: o → ue), {{irse}} (to leave, to head off). You already know one: {{llamarse}}, as in {{me llamo}}.

**Where the pronoun goes.** Before a conjugated verb: {{Me levanto temprano.}} With an infinitive you can also put it on the end: {{Voy a levantarme temprano}} or {{Me voy a levantar temprano}}, both right. With {{no}}: {{No me levanto temprano.}}
**Parts of the body** take {{el}}, {{la}}, not “my”, because the {{me}} already says whose: {{Me lavo los dientes.}} “I brush my teeth.” {{Me lavo las manos.}} “I wash my hands.”

ex.t: Me despierto a las seis, pero me levanto a las seis y media.
ex.tr: I wake up at six, but I get up at six thirty.
My son gets dressed by himself.
What time do you go to bed?
We're leaving at eight.
I'm going to take a shower.

blocks.tip: Some verbs change their meaning with {{se}}: {{ir}} “to go”, {{irse}} “to leave”; {{dormir}} “to sleep”, {{dormirse}} “to fall asleep”: {{Me duermo a las once.}} “I fall asleep at eleven.”

mistakes.why: {{levantarse}} needs {{me}}: without it, {{levanto}} means “I lift (something)”.
With parts of the body: {{los}}, not {{mis}}. The {{me}} already says whose.

mistakes.tr: I'm going to take a shower.
mistakes.why: The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb ({{Me voy a bañar}}) or on the end of the infinitive ({{bañarme}}), never between them.

lessons.title: Say what's happening right now
lessons.summary: Say what you're doing at this moment, on the phone or in a text: “I can't talk right now: I'm driving.”
lessons.topic: {{estar}} + the -ando / -iendo form ({{estoy comiendo}}); where pronouns go with it

goal.t: Ahorita no puedo hablar: estoy manejando.
goal.tr: I can't talk right now: I'm driving.

dialog.t: ¿Qué estás haciendo?
dialog.tr: What are you doing?

dialog.t: Estoy cocinando. ¿Por qué?
dialog.tr: I'm cooking. Why?

dialog.t: Tu papá y yo estamos saliendo de la casa. Vamos para allá.
dialog.tr: Your dad and I are leaving the house. We're on our way over.

dialog.t: ¡Ay, no! Los niños se están bañando y la casa es un desastre.
dialog.tr: Oh, no! The kids are in the bath and the house is a mess.

dialog.t: No importa, hija. ¡Ahí vamos!
dialog.tr: It doesn't matter, sweetheart. We're coming!

blocks.p: **Right now.** {{estar}} + a verb ending in **-ando** or **-iendo** says what is happening at this moment: {{Estoy manejando.}} “I'm driving.” Only {{estar}} changes: {{estoy}}, {{estás}}, {{está}}, {{estamos}}, {{están}}.

blocks.means: the “-ing” form of a verb. In Spanish it ends in -ando or -iendo: {{hablando}} “speaking”, {{comiendo}} “eating”.

blocks.p: **Making it.** -ar verbs: drop -ar and add **-ando**: {{hablar}} → {{hablando}}. -er and -ir verbs: add **-iendo**: {{comer}} → {{comiendo}}, {{escribir}} → {{escribiendo}}. It never changes for the person.

After a vowel, the i of -iendo becomes **y**: {{leer}} → {{leyendo}}, {{traer}} → {{trayendo}}, {{oír}} → {{oyendo}}. And -ir verbs that change e → i or o → ue change here too, to i and u: {{pedir}} → {{pidiendo}}, {{vestir}} → {{vistiendo}}, {{dormir}} → {{durmiendo}}.

**When not to use it.** English uses “-ing” much more than Spanish does. For habits and for plans, Spanish uses the plain present or {{ir a}}: {{Trabajo en un banco}} “I'm working at a bank (these days)”, {{Mañana voy a trabajar}} “I'm working tomorrow”. Keep {{estar}} + -ando for what is really in progress.
**Pronouns** go before {{estar}}, or on the end of the gerund, which then takes an accent mark: {{Me estoy bañando}} or {{Estoy bañándome}}.

ex.t: ¿Qué estás haciendo? — Nada, estoy viendo la tele.
ex.tr: What are you doing? — Nothing, I'm watching TV.
It's raining hard.

ex.t: Mis papás están viajando por Europa.
ex.tr: My parents are traveling around Europe.
We're waiting for the bus.
ex.note: {{esperar}} “to wait for”, with no word for “for”

ex.tr: The baby is sleeping.
Are you listening to me?

blocks.tip: {{Ahorita}} is Mexican for “right now”, but careful: it can also mean “in a little while”, or even “later, maybe”. {{¡Ahorita voy!}} may mean you're not going just yet.

mistakes.why: After {{estoy}}, the gerund: {{trabajando}}.
For plans Spanish uses {{ir a}} (or the present: {{Mañana trabajo}}), not {{estar}} + -ando.
After a vowel, the i of -iendo becomes y: {{leyendo}}.

lessons.title: Say how often, and never
lessons.summary: Say how often you do things, and use “never”, “nothing” and “nobody” the Spanish way: “I hardly ever eat meat.”
lessons.topic: {{siempre, a veces, casi nunca, nunca}}; {{todos los días}}, {{una vez a la semana}}; {{no… nada / nadie / nunca}}

goal.t: Casi nunca como carne, pero siempre tomo café.
goal.tr: I hardly ever eat meat, but I always drink coffee.

dialog.t: ¿Hace ejercicio?
dialog.tr: Do you exercise?

dialog.t: Sí, voy al gimnasio dos veces a la semana.
dialog.tr: Yes, I go to the gym twice a week.

dialog.t: ¿Fuma?
dialog.tr: Do you smoke?

dialog.t: No, nunca.
dialog.tr: No, never.

dialog.t: ¿Y toma alcohol?
dialog.tr: And do you drink alcohol?

dialog.t: A veces, los fines de semana. Pero entre semana no tomo nada.
dialog.tr: Sometimes, on weekends. But during the week I don't drink anything.

blocks.p: **How often.** From most to least: {{siempre}} (always), {{casi siempre}} (almost always), {{normalmente}} (usually), {{a veces}} (sometimes), {{casi nunca}} (hardly ever), {{nunca}} (never). They usually go before the verb: {{Siempre desayuno en casa.}}

**Every…, once a…** {{todos los días}} (every day), {{todas las noches}} (every night), {{cada semana}} (every week), {{una vez a la semana}} (once a week), {{dos veces al mes}} (twice a month), {{los lunes}} (on Mondays).

**Never, nothing, nobody.** Spanish has two ways to say them: the negative word alone before the verb ({{Nunca como carne.}}), or {{no}} before the verb and the negative word after it ({{No como carne nunca.}}). So Spanish happily doubles its negatives, and must do it when the negative word comes after the verb: {{No hay nada.}} “There's nothing.”

table: {{No quiero nada.}} I don't want anything.
{{Nunca voy.}} / {{No voy nunca.}} I never go.

ex.tr: I'm always late.
Sometimes I work on Saturdays.

ex.t: No hay nadie en la oficina.
ex.tr: There's nobody in the office.
Do you want anything? — No, nothing, thanks.
My son never eats vegetables.

ex.t: Vamos al cine una vez al mes.
ex.tr: We go to the movies once a month.
I don't know anything about soccer.

blocks.tip: {{Nunca}} and {{nada}} stand alone as answers: {{¿Qué haces? — Nada.}} “What are you doing? — Nothing.” {{¿Vas al gimnasio? — Nunca.}}

mistakes.why: After {{no}}, Spanish uses the negative word: {{nada}}, not {{algo}}.
With the negative word after the verb, {{no}} must come before the verb.
{{nunca}} goes before the verb, or after it with {{no}} in front: {{No como carne nunca}}.

lessons.title: Make small talk about the weather
lessons.summary: Talk about the weather the way Mexicans do: “It's so hot today!” “Yes, and it's going to rain this afternoon.”
lessons.topic: {{hace calor}}, {{hace frío}}; {{está nublado}}; {{llueve}}, {{está lloviendo}}; {{tener calor}} and {{tener frío}}

goal.t: ¡Qué calor hace hoy! — Sí, y en la tarde va a llover.
goal.tr: It's so hot today! — Yes, and it's going to rain this afternoon.

dialog.t: ¡Qué frío hace hoy!
dialog.tr: It's so cold today!

dialog.t: Sí, y está muy nublado. ¿Va a llover?
dialog.tr: Yes, and it's very cloudy. Is it going to rain?

dialog.t: Creo que sí. En esta época siempre llueve en la noche.
dialog.tr: I think so. At this time of year it always rains at night.

dialog.t: Pues voy por mi suéter. Tengo mucho frío.
dialog.tr: Well, I'm going to get my sweater. I'm really cold.

blocks.p: **Three ways to talk about the weather.** {{hacer}} with what you feel (heat, cold, wind, sun), {{estar}} with how the sky looks, and the weather's own verbs for rain and snow. There's no “it”: the verb is enough.

table: {{Va a llover.}} It's going to rain.
{{Hace buen tiempo.}} The weather is nice.
{{Va a nevar.}} It's going to snow.

blocks.p: {{calor}} and {{frío}} are nouns here (heat, cold), so “very” is {{mucho}}, not {{muy}}: {{Hace mucho calor.}} And {{¡Qué calor!}} “It's so hot!” is how many conversations start. {{hay}} works for what's in the air: {{Hay neblina}} (it's foggy), {{Hay mucha humedad}} (it's very humid).
**The weather, you, or a thing?** For the weather: {{hacer}}. For how **you** feel: {{tener}}. For a thing you touch: {{estar}}. English says “hot” and “cold” for all three; Spanish doesn't:

table: {{El café está caliente.}} The coffee is hot.
{{La sopa está fría.}} The soup is cold.

ex.tr: It's very hot today.
It's raining. Do you have an umbrella?

ex.t: En Monterrey hace mucho calor en verano.
ex.tr: In Monterrey it's very hot in summer.
It's going to be cold tomorrow.
Are you cold? I'll lend you my jacket.
What's the weather like in your city?

blocks.tip: Seasons: {{la primavera}} (spring), {{el verano}} (summer), {{el otoño}} (fall), {{el invierno}} (winter). In much of Mexico people talk more about {{la época de lluvias}}, the rainy season, roughly June to October.

mistakes.why: Weather you feel: {{hace}}. No “it”, and no {{es}}.
How you feel: {{tener}} + {{calor}} or {{frío}}.
Here {{frío}} is a noun, “cold”: {{mucho}}, not {{muy}}.

practice.tr: It's very windy today.
Are you cold? — Yes, I'm really cold.

practice.q: You touch your coffee: it's gone cold. You say…

lines.tr: And they say it's going to rain tomorrow.

lessons.title: Talk about people and things you know
lessons.summary: Say who and what you know, and what you know how to do: “Do you know my friend Paola? She can speak four languages.”
lessons.topic: {{saber}} (facts, how to) and {{conocer}} (people, places); the personal {{a}}

goal.t: ¿Conoces a mi amiga Paola? Sabe hablar cuatro idiomas.
goal.tr: Do you know my friend Paola? She can speak four languages.

dialog.t: ¿Conoces a alguien aquí?
dialog.tr: Do you know anyone here?

dialog.t: No, no conozco a nadie. ¿Sabes dónde está la oficina de Recursos Humanos?
dialog.tr: No, I don't know anybody. Do you know where the HR office is?

dialog.t: Sí, está en el segundo piso. ¿Y conoces la ciudad?
dialog.tr: Yes, it's on the second floor. And do you know the city?

dialog.t: Un poco. Pero no sé manejar, entonces voy en metro.
dialog.tr: A little. But I can't drive, so I take the subway.

dialog.t: Yo tampoco sé manejar. ¡Vamos juntos!
dialog.tr: I can't drive either. Let's go together!

blocks.p: **Two verbs for “to know”.** {{saber}} is to know a fact, or to know how to do something. {{conocer}} is to know a person or a place: to be familiar with it, to have met it or been there.

table: {{Sé su nombre.}} I know her name.
{{¿Sabes dónde vive?}} Do you know where he lives?
{{¿Conoces Oaxaca?}} Have you been to Oaxaca?
{{No conozco este restaurante.}} I don't know this restaurant.

blocks.p: Both are irregular only for “I”: {{sé}} (with an accent), {{sabes}}, {{sabe}}, {{sabemos}}, {{saben}}; {{conozco}}, {{conoces}}, {{conoce}}, {{conocemos}}, {{conocen}}.

**{{saber}} + infinitive** is “to know how to”, the usual way to talk about a skill: {{Sé cocinar}} “I can cook”, {{¿Sabes bailar salsa?}} “Can you dance salsa?”. {{poder}} is for being able or allowed at the moment: {{Hoy no puedo nadar: hace mucho frío.}}

blocks.means: the person or thing that a verb is done to: in “I see Juan”, Juan; in “I buy bread”, bread.

blocks.p: **The personal {{a}}.** When the object is a particular person (or a much-loved pet), Spanish puts {{a}} in front of it. English has nothing there: it doesn't mean “to”, it just marks the person.

table: {{Veo la casa.}} I see the house.
{{Busco mi celular.}} I'm looking for my phone.
{{Busco a mi hijo.}} I'm looking for my son.
{{Conozco a tu hermana.}} I know your sister.

ex.tr: Do you know what time it is?

ex.t: No conozco a nadie en esta ciudad.
ex.tr: I don't know anybody in this city.
My daughter can already read.
Have you met my parents?
I don't know. I'll ask.

ex.t: Visitamos a la abuela los domingos.
ex.tr: We visit Grandma on Sundays.
I want to visit Chiapas.
ex.note: {{conocer}} a place: to go there for the first time

blocks.tip: {{Mucho gusto en conocerte}} “Nice to meet you” uses {{conocer}}: meeting someone for the first time. {{¿Ya se conocen?}} “Have you two met?”

mistakes.why: Knowing a person: {{conocer}}.
Knowing how to do something: {{saber}} + infinitive.

mistakes.right: Veo a mi mamá los domingos.
mistakes.tr: I see my mom on Sundays.
mistakes.why: A particular person as the object takes the personal {{a}}.

practice.tr: Do you know where the bathroom is?
I don't know your boyfriend.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.summary: Say what's bigger, cheaper or better, and what's the best: “My brother is taller than me, but I'm older.”
lessons.topic: {{más … que}}, {{menos … que}}, {{tan … como}}; {{mejor, peor, mayor, menor}}; {{el más … de}}

goal.t: Mi hermano es más alto que yo, pero yo soy mayor.
goal.tr: My brother is taller than me, but I'm older.

dialog.t: ¿Cuál es mejor, este o ese?
dialog.tr: Which one is better, this one or that one?

dialog.t: Este es más caro, pero es más rápido.
dialog.tr: This one is more expensive, but it's faster.

dialog.t: ¿Y la cámara?
dialog.tr: And the camera?

dialog.t: La cámara de ese es tan buena como la de este. Y ese es el más barato de la tienda.
dialog.tr: That one's camera is as good as this one's. And that one is the cheapest in the store.

dialog.t: Entonces quiero ese.
dialog.tr: Then I'll take that one.

blocks.p: **More and less.** {{más}} + adjective + {{que}}: {{más alto que}} “taller than”, {{más caro que}} “more expensive than”. Spanish has no “-er”: everything takes {{más}}. The opposite is {{menos … que}} “less … than”. The adjective still agrees: {{Las playas de aquí son más bonitas.}}

**As … as.** {{tan}} + adjective + {{como}}: {{Es tan alto como su papá.}} “He's as tall as his dad.” With a noun, {{tanto}} + noun + {{como}}, matching the noun: {{No tengo tanto dinero como tú.}} {{No trabajo tantas horas como tú.}}
**Four irregular ones.** Like English “better”, these don't use {{más}}:
{{mayor}} and {{menor}} are for people's age; for things, {{más viejo}} and {{más nuevo}}. In the plural they add -es: {{mejores}}, {{peores}}, {{mayores}}.

**The most.** {{el}}, {{la}}, {{los}} or {{las}} + noun + {{más}} + adjective, and “in” after it is {{de}}: {{el edificio más alto de la ciudad}} “the tallest building in the city”, {{la mejor comida del mundo}} “the best food in the world” ({{mejor}} and {{peor}} go before the noun).

ex.t: El metro es más rápido que el camión.
ex.tr: The subway is faster than the bus.

ex.t: Esta playera es menos cara que esa.
ex.tr: This T-shirt is less expensive than that one.

ex.t: Mi hija es tan alta como yo.
ex.tr: My daughter is as tall as I am.

ex.t: Es el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.
ex.tr: It's the best restaurant in town.

ex.t: Mi abuelo es el mayor de la familia.
ex.tr: My grandfather is the oldest in the family.

ex.t: Hoy hace más calor que ayer.
ex.tr: It's hotter today than yesterday.
I work more than you do.

blocks.tip: After {{que}} and {{como}}, Spanish uses {{yo}} and {{tú}}, not “me”: {{más alto que yo}} “taller than me”, {{tan cansada como tú}}.

mistakes.wrong: Es más grande de mi casa.
mistakes.right: Es más grande que mi casa.
mistakes.why: “Than” is {{que}}. ({{de}} is the “in” after “the most”, and comes before numbers: {{más de cien}}.)

mistakes.wrong: Este celular es más bueno que ese.
mistakes.right: Este celular es mejor que ese.
mistakes.tr: This phone is better than that one.
mistakes.why: For quality, “better” is {{mejor}}.

mistakes.wrong: Es el más alto edificio de la ciudad.
mistakes.right: Es el edificio más alto de la ciudad.
mistakes.tr: It's the tallest building in the city.
mistakes.why: The noun first, then {{más}} + adjective; and “in” is {{de}}.

lessons.title: Say “it” and “them”
lessons.summary: Talk about something without repeating its name: “Where's my phone? I can't find it.”
lessons.topic: direct object pronouns {{lo, la, los, las}} (and {{me, te, nos}}); where they go

goal.t: ¿Dónde está mi celular? No lo encuentro.
goal.tr: Where's my phone? I can't find it.

dialog.t: ¿Tienes las llaves?
dialog.tr: Do you have the keys?

dialog.t: Sí, las tengo.
dialog.tr: Yes, I have them.

dialog.t: ¿Y los boletos?
dialog.tr: And the tickets?

dialog.t: No, no los tengo. ¿Tú los tienes?
dialog.tr: No, I don't have them. Do you?

dialog.t: Mmm… Creo que están en la mesa. Ahorita los traigo.
dialog.tr: Hmm… I think they're on the table. I'll go get them.

blocks.p: **Not repeating.** Instead of saying {{el celular}} again, Spanish uses a short pronoun, and it goes **before the verb**: {{No lo encuentro.}} “I can't find it”, word for word “not it I-find”.

blocks.means: a short word that stands for the object of a verb: it, them, him, her. In Spanish: {{lo, la, los, las}}, and {{me, te, nos}}.

blocks.p: **It matches the noun it stands for**, in gender and number:

The same pronouns stand for people: {{lo}} “him” (and polite “you”, to a man), {{la}} “her” (and polite “you”, to a woman), {{los}}, {{las}} “them”: {{¿Conoces a Pablo? — Sí, lo conozco.}} For “me”, “you” and “us”: {{me}}, {{te}}, {{nos}}: {{¿Me ves?}} “Can you see me?” {{Te quiero.}} “I love you.”

**Where it goes.** Before a conjugated verb: {{Lo compro.}} With an infinitive or a gerund, either before the first verb or joined to the end: {{Lo voy a comprar}} = {{Voy a comprarlo}} “I'm going to buy it”; {{La estoy buscando}} = {{Estoy buscándola}} “I'm looking for it”. With {{no}}: {{No lo sé.}} “I don't know.”

ex.t: ¿Dónde compras las tortillas? — Las compro en la tortillería.
ex.tr: Where do you buy tortillas? — I buy them at the tortilla shop.
I'll call you tomorrow.
ex.note: the present, for something you're about to do

ex.tr: Can you hear me? — Yes, I can hear you.

ex.t: Mi abuela nos visita cada domingo.
ex.tr: My grandmother visits us every Sunday.
I don't know.
ex.note: word for word “I don't know it”: very common

ex.t: La película es muy buena. Tienes que verla.
ex.tr: The movie is really good. You have to see it.

ex.t: ¿Las invitaciones? Las voy a mandar hoy.
ex.tr: The invitations? I'm going to send them today.

blocks.tip: Mexicans use {{lo}} for “him”: {{Lo conozco}} “I know him”. (In Spain you'll also hear {{le}} there.)

{{las llaves}} is feminine and plural: {{las}}.
Before {{voy}} ({{Lo voy a comprar}}) or joined to the infinitive ({{comprarlo}}), never between them.

lessons.summary: Give, lend, tell and send things to people: “I'm going to send my brother a message.” “Can you pass me the salt?”
lessons.topic: indirect object pronouns {{me, te, le, nos, les}}; {{dar, decir, mandar, prestar, pasar}}; {{le}} with {{a}} + the person

dialog.t: Yo no tengo dinero. ¿Me prestas cien pesos?
dialog.tr: I don't have any money. Can you lend me a hundred pesos?

dialog.t: Bueno, te presto cien. Pero me los pagas el viernes.
dialog.tr: Okay, I'll lend you a hundred. But you pay me back on Friday.

blocks.means: the person who receives something, or for whom something is done: in “I give Ana a present”, Ana.

blocks.p: **To whom, for whom.** Verbs like give, tell, send and lend have two objects: the thing, and the person who gets it. That person is the indirect object, and it has its own pronouns, which go before the verb:

table: {{¿Me das tu número?}} Will you give me your number?
{{Te mando la dirección.}} I'll send you the address.
{{Le digo la verdad.}} I tell him the truth.
{{Nos prestan su carro.}} They lend us their car.
{{Les doy las gracias.}} I thank them.

blocks.p: You know these pronouns already: they're the ones in {{me gusta}}, {{te gusta}}, {{le gusta}}. With {{gustar}}, the person is an indirect object too: “it pleases **to me**”.

**{{le}} and {{a}} + the person, together.** Spanish usually says both: {{Le doy un regalo a mi mamá.}} “I give my mom a present.” {{Les mando un correo a mis jefes.}} It looks repeated, but that's normal Spanish.

**{{dar}}** “to give” is irregular for “I”: {{doy}}, {{das}}, {{da}}, {{damos}}, {{dan}}. Other verbs that take a person this way: {{decir}} (to tell), {{mandar}} (to send), {{prestar}} (to lend), {{pasar}} (to pass), {{traer}} (to bring), {{enseñar}} (to show, to teach), {{preguntar}} (to ask), {{regalar}} (to give as a present), {{comprar}} (to buy for). They go in the same places as {{lo}}: {{Le voy a mandar}} = {{Voy a mandarle}}.

ex.tr: Can you pass me the salt, please?
Can I borrow your pen?

ex.tr: I'm going to buy my girlfriend a present.

lessons.title: Say what hurts and what you need
lessons.summary: At the doctor's or in a store: say what hurts, what you love, what's missing and how clothes fit: “My throat really hurts.”
lessons.topic: verbs like {{gustar}}: {{doler, encantar, interesar, importar, faltar, quedar}}

goal.t: Me duele mucho la garganta y tengo un poco de fiebre.
goal.tr: My throat really hurts and I have a bit of a fever.

dialog.t: ¿Qué le pasa?
dialog.tr: What's the matter?

dialog.t: Me duele mucho la cabeza y me duelen los ojos.
dialog.tr: I have a bad headache and my eyes hurt.

dialog.t: ¿Desde cuándo?

blocks.p: **Back to front, again.** You know {{Me gusta el café}}: the thing is the subject, and {{me}} says who. Several common verbs work exactly the same way:

table: My head hurts. I have a headache.
I don't mind. I don't care.

blocks.p: As with {{gustar}}, the verb matches the thing: {{Me duele el pie}} “my foot hurts”, {{Me duelen los pies}} “my feet hurt”; {{Me encantan los tamales}}. And {{a}} + the person names who: {{A mi hijo le duele el estómago.}}
**Parts of the body take {{el}}, {{la}}**, not “my”: {{Me duele la espalda}} “My back hurts”. The {{me}} already says whose back it is.

**{{quedar}}** has two everyday uses. For clothes, how they fit: {{¿Cómo me queda?}} “How does it look on me?”, {{Te queda muy bien}} “It looks great on you”, {{Me queda chico}} “It's too small for me”. And what's left: {{Nos quedan diez minutos}} “We have ten minutes left”.

ex.t: A mi esposo le duele la espalda.
ex.tr: My husband's back hurts.

ex.tr: I love Oaxacan food.
Are you into soccer?
We don't have enough time.
These pants are too big for me.

lessons.title: Say what you did yesterday
lessons.summary: Tell someone what you did yesterday, last night or last week: “Yesterday I worked late and had dinner at home.”
lessons.topic: the preterite of regular verbs ({{hablé, comí, viví}}); {{ayer, anoche, el … pasado}}; {{¿Ya…?}}

goal.t: Ayer trabajé hasta tarde y cené en casa.
goal.tr: Yesterday I worked late and had dinner at home.

dialog.t: ¿Cómo te fue el fin de semana?
dialog.tr: How was your weekend?

dialog.t: Muy bien. El sábado limpié la casa y en la noche cenamos con unos amigos.
dialog.tr: Really good. On Saturday I cleaned the house, and in the evening we had dinner with some friends.

dialog.t: ¿Y el domingo?
dialog.tr: And on Sunday?

dialog.t: Descansé todo el día. ¿Y tú?

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: present, past, future.

blocks.p: **The past of finished events.** Spanish has two main past tenses. This one, the preterite, tells what happened: actions that started and finished, often one after another: “I worked”, “we had dinner”, “she called”.

blocks.means: the Spanish past tense for finished events: {{trabajé}} “I worked”, {{comí}} “I ate”.

blocks.p: **The accent marks matter.** {{trabajo}} is “I work”; {{trabajó}}, stressed on the end, is “he worked”. Say the last syllable loud: {{hablé}} (ha-BLÉ), {{habló}} (ha-BLÓ). -er and -ir verbs share one set of endings.
**“We” looks like the present** for -ar and -ir verbs: {{trabajamos}}, {{vivimos}}. A word like {{ayer}} makes it clear: {{Ayer trabajamos mucho.}}

**Spelling, in “I” only.** To keep their sound, three endings change their spelling: -car → -qué ({{buscar}} → {{busqué}}), -gar → -gué ({{llegar}} → {{llegué}}, {{pagar}} → {{pagué}}), -zar → -cé ({{empezar}} → {{empecé}}). Stem-changing -ar and -er verbs don't change in the preterite: {{pensé}}, {{volví}}.

**When.** {{ayer}} (yesterday), {{anoche}} (last night), {{anteayer}} (the day before yesterday), {{el lunes}} (on Monday), {{la semana pasada}} (last week), {{el año pasado}} (last year), {{hace dos días}} (two days ago).

ex.tr: Last night I had dinner with my parents.
What time did you get here?

ex.t: Mi hermana vivió en Canadá dos años.
ex.tr: My sister lived in Canada for two years.
I got here late and didn't have breakfast.
Have you eaten yet?
ex.note: Mexicans use the preterite for things done today, too

ex.t: La semana pasada compramos un sofá.
ex.tr: Last week we bought a couch.
Did you all like the movie?

blocks.tip: {{¿Ya…?}} “already, yet” with the preterite is the everyday Mexican way to ask if something is done: {{¿Ya pagaste?}} “Have you paid?” {{Ya terminé.}} “I'm done.”

mistakes.why: A finished action in the past: the preterite, {{trabajé}}.
Without the accent, {{hablo}} is “I speak”. “She spoke”: {{habló}}.
-gar verbs add a u in “I” to keep the hard g: {{llegué}}.

lessons.title: Say where you went and what you did
lessons.summary: Talk about trips and outings with the four irregular pasts you'll use most: “I went to the beach with my friends.”
lessons.topic: the preterite of {{ir}} and {{ser}} ({{fui}}), {{hacer}} ({{hice}}), {{tener}} ({{tuve}}), {{estar}} ({{estuve}})

goal.t: ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana? — Fui a la playa con mis amigos.
goal.tr: What did you do last weekend? — I went to the beach with my friends.

dialog.t: ¿Qué hiciste en vacaciones?
dialog.tr: What did you do on vacation?

dialog.t: Fui a Oaxaca con mi familia.
dialog.tr: I went to Oaxaca with my family.

dialog.t: ¡Qué padre! ¿Y cómo estuvo?
dialog.tr: How cool! And how was it?

dialog.t: Estuvo increíble. Hicimos muchas cosas y comimos muy bien.
dialog.tr: It was amazing. We did lots of things and ate really well.

dialog.t: ¿Cuánto tiempo estuvieron allá?
dialog.tr: How long were you there?

dialog.t: Una semana. Pero tuvimos que regresar el domingo.

blocks.p: **Four irregular pasts for every day.** They have their own stems, and their endings take **no accent mark**:

**{{ir}} and {{ser}} share one past.** {{fui}} is both “I went” and “I was”; the sentence tells you which: {{Fui al cine}} “I went to the movies”, {{Fue un día muy bonito}} “It was a lovely day”. With {{ir}} there's nearly always an {{a}}.
**{{hizo}}** is written with a z, to keep the sound of {{hice}}. And {{¿Qué hiciste?}} “What did you do?” is one of the most useful questions in Spanish.

**How was it?** Mexicans ask {{¿Cómo te fue?}} “How did it go (for you)?” and {{¿Cómo estuvo?}} “How was it?” about a trip, a party or a movie. Answers: {{¡Muy bien!}}, {{Estuvo padrísimo}} (it was great), {{Me fue mal}} (it went badly).

ex.tr: We went to the movies on Saturday.
How did your exam go?
It was really hot yesterday.

ex.t: Estuve en casa todo el día.

I had to work on Sunday.

ex.t: La fiesta fue en casa de Pepe.
ex.tr: The party was at Pepe's place.

ex.t: Mis hijos ya hicieron la tarea.
ex.tr: My kids already did their homework.

blocks.tip: {{tener que}} in the past says what you had to do: {{Tuve que ir al doctor.}} “I had to go to the doctor.”

mistakes.why: These short pasts take no accent mark: {{fui}}, {{fue}}.
{{hacer}} has its own past: {{hice}}.
With a z: {{hizo}}.

lessons.summary: Tell what happened, with more of the everyday irregular pasts: “My cousins came, and we showed them around the city.”
lessons.topic: more irregular preterites ({{pude, puse, quise, supe, vine, dije, traje}}; {{di, vi}}); {{leyó}}; {{pidió, durmió}}

goal.t: Vinieron mis primos y les enseñamos la ciudad.

dialog.t: ¿Fuiste a la boda de Marisol?
dialog.tr: Did you go to Marisol's wedding?

dialog.t: No, no pude. Mi hijo se enfermó.
dialog.tr: No, I couldn't. My son got sick.

dialog.t: ¡Ay, qué mal! ¿Y cómo está?
dialog.tr: Oh, that's too bad! How is he?

dialog.t: Ya está mejor. Durmió mucho, y el domingo vino el doctor.
dialog.tr: He's better now. He slept a lot, and on Sunday the doctor came.

dialog.t: Qué bueno. Oye, ¿viste las fotos de la boda?
dialog.tr: Good. Hey, did you see the wedding photos?

dialog.t: Sí, Marisol me las mandó. ¡Me dijo que la fiesta estuvo increíble!
dialog.tr: Yes, Marisol sent them to me. She told me the party was amazing!

blocks.p: **The strong pasts.** A group of common verbs take a new stem in the preterite, and share one set of endings, again with **no accent marks**: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron.
After a j, “they” drops the i: {{dijeron}}, {{trajeron}}. The others keep it: {{pudieron}}, {{vinieron}}.
**{{dar}} and {{ver}}** take the -er/-ir endings, without accents: {{di}}, {{diste}}, {{dio}}, {{dimos}}, {{dieron}}; {{vi}}, {{viste}}, {{vio}}, {{vimos}}, {{vieron}}.
**A y in the middle.** When the stem ends in a vowel, “he, she” and “they” get a y: {{leer}} → {{leyó}}, {{leyeron}}; {{oír}} → {{oyó}}; {{creer}} → {{creyó}}; {{caerse}} (to fall) → {{se cayó}}.

**-ir stem-changers** change only in “he, she” and “they”, e → i and o → u: {{pedir}} → {{pidió}}, {{pidieron}}; {{dormir}} → {{durmió}}, {{durmieron}}; {{sentirse}} → {{se sintió}}; {{preferir}} → {{prefirió}}. “I” is regular: {{pedí}}, {{dormí}}.

**{{supe}} and {{no pude}}.** In the preterite, {{saber}} often means “found out”: {{Supe la noticia ayer}} “I heard the news yesterday”. And {{no pude}} means you tried and couldn't: {{No pude dormir.}}

After a j, “they” is -eron: {{dijeron}}, {{trajeron}}.

lessons.title: Say what life used to be like
lessons.summary: Talk about your childhood and how things used to be: “When I was a kid, I lived in a small town and played in the street all day.”
lessons.topic: the imperfect ({{-aba}}, {{-ía}}); {{era}}, {{iba}}, {{veía}}; {{había}}; habits and descriptions in the past

goal.t: Cuando era niño, vivía en un pueblo y jugaba en la calle todo el día.
goal.tr: When I was a kid, I lived in a small town and played in the street all day.

dialog.t: Abuela, ¿cómo era tu vida cuando eras joven?
dialog.tr: Grandma, what was your life like when you were young?

dialog.t: Era muy diferente. Vivíamos en un rancho y no había luz.
dialog.tr: It was very different. We lived on a ranch and there was no electricity.

dialog.t: ¿Y qué hacían en la noche?
dialog.tr: And what did you all do at night?

blocks.p: **A second past.** The preterite tells what happened. This one describes how things **were**, and what used to happen again and again: “we lived on a ranch”, “my dad used to tell stories”, “there was no electricity”. It paints the background.

blocks.means: the Spanish past tense for how things were and what used to happen: {{vivía}} “I lived, I used to live”.

blocks.p: Good news: it's the most regular tense in Spanish. No stem changes ({{quería}}, {{podía}}, {{dormía}}), and “I” and “he, she” are the same, so name the person when it isn't clear. Mind the accent marks: {{trabajábamos}}, and every -ía.
**Only three irregular verbs:**
“There was, there were”, in a description, is {{había}} (the past of {{hay}}), and like {{hay}} it never changes: {{Había muchos árboles.}}

**What it's for:** habits, English “used to” or “would” ({{Los domingos íbamos al parque}}); descriptions of people, places and states ({{La casa era grande}}, {{Estaba cansado}}); age and the time ({{Tenía diez años}}, {{Eran las ocho}}).

ex.t: Cuando era niña, quería ser doctora.
ex.tr: When I was a little girl, I wanted to be a doctor.
My grandparents lived in Zacatecas.
I used to work at a bank.

ex.tr: On Sundays we would go to my aunt's house.

lessons.summary: Tell what happened, with the scene around it: “I was in the shower when the phone rang.”
lessons.topic: preterite or imperfect: the events and the scene; {{estaba}} + -ando; {{cuando}}, {{mientras}}, {{de repente}}

goal.t: Estaba en la regadera cuando sonó el teléfono.
goal.tr: I was in the shower when the phone rang.

dialog.t: ¿Qué te pasó? ¿Por qué llegaste tarde?
dialog.tr: What happened to you? Why were you late?

dialog.t: Ay, iba en el camión y de repente se descompuso.
dialog.tr: Ugh, I was on the bus and suddenly it broke down.

dialog.t: ¡No! ¿Y qué hiciste?
dialog.tr: No! And what did you do?

dialog.t: Estaba lloviendo, entonces tomé un taxi. Pero había mucho tráfico.
dialog.tr: It was raining, so I took a taxi. But there was a lot of traffic.

dialog.t: ¡Qué mala suerte!
dialog.tr: What bad luck!

blocks.p: **Two pasts in one story.** A story needs both. The **imperfect** sets the scene: what was going on, how things were, the time, the weather, how people felt. The **preterite** moves the story on: what happened, and then what happened next.

table: {{Tomé un taxi.}} I took a taxi.
{{Estaba muy cansada.}} I was very tired.
{{Me dormí en el sofá.}} I fell asleep on the couch.
{{Íbamos a la playa.}} We were on our way to the beach.
{{Vimos un accidente.}} We saw an accident.

blocks.p: **Interrupted.** For something in progress that another event interrupts: {{estaba}} + -ando (or the plain imperfect), then {{cuando}} and the preterite: {{Estaba cocinando cuando llegaron mis suegros.}} “I was cooking when my in-laws arrived.” Two things going on at the same time: imperfect + {{mientras}} + imperfect: {{Mientras yo cocinaba, los niños jugaban.}}

**A quick test.** Could you say “at that moment, it was going on”? Imperfect. Could you say “and then”? Preterite. Words like {{de repente}} (suddenly), {{entonces}} (so, then), {{luego}} and {{después}} (then, afterwards) and {{al final}} (in the end) usually bring the preterite.

ex.t: Cuando llegué a la fiesta, todos estaban bailando.
ex.tr: When I got to the party, everyone was dancing.

ex.t: Hacía mucho frío, entonces nos quedamos en casa.
ex.tr: It was very cold, so we stayed home.

ex.t: Estábamos en el parque cuando empezó a llover.
ex.tr: We were at the park when it started to rain.

ex.t: Mientras yo trabajaba, mi esposa cuidaba a los niños.
ex.tr: While I was working, my wife looked after the kids.

ex.t: No fui a clase porque estaba enfermo.
ex.tr: I didn't go to class because I was sick.

ex.t: Mi hijo se cayó cuando estaba jugando.
ex.tr: My son fell while he was playing.

blocks.tip: Two phrases that keep a story going: {{¿Qué pasó?}} “What happened?” and {{¿Y luego?}} “And then what?”

mistakes.wrong: Estuve en la regadera cuando sonaba el teléfono.
mistakes.right: Estaba en la regadera cuando sonó el teléfono.
mistakes.tr: I was in the shower when the phone rang.
mistakes.why: The scene (where you were): imperfect. The event that interrupts it: preterite.

mistakes.wrong: Cuando era niño, un día me rompía el brazo.
mistakes.right: Cuando era niño, un día me rompí el brazo.
mistakes.tr: When I was a kid, I broke my arm one day.
mistakes.why: {{un día}} marks a single event: the preterite.

{{Mientras yo lavé los platos, él vio la tele.}}

options: Porque estaba muy cansada y me dormí.
Porque estuve muy cansada y me dormía.

answers.tr: I was at the supermarket and suddenly I saw my high school teacher.

lessons.title: Say how long ago and how long
lessons.summary: Say when something happened and how long it's been going on: “I came three years ago.” “I've lived here for three years.”
lessons.topic: {{hace}} + time (ago); for and since: {{hace … que}} + present, {{desde}}, {{llevar}}

goal.t: Vivo en México desde hace tres años.
goal.tr: I've been living in Mexico for three years.

dialog.t: ¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives aquí?
dialog.tr: How long have you lived here?

dialog.t: Dos años. Llegué hace dos años, en enero.
dialog.tr: Two years. I came two years ago, in January.

dialog.t: ¿Y estudias español desde entonces?
dialog.tr: And have you been studying Spanish since then?

dialog.t: Sí, llevo dos años estudiando. ¿Y tú? ¿Desde cuándo trabajas aquí?
dialog.tr: Yes, I've been studying for two years. And you? Since when have you worked here?

dialog.t: Desde 2019. ¡Hace mucho!
dialog.tr: Since 2019. A long time!

blocks.p: **Ago: {{hace}} + time**, with the preterite: {{Llegué hace tres años.}} “I came three years ago.” {{¿Cuándo la conociste? — Hace un mes.}} Here {{hace}} has nothing to do with doing or the weather: it means “ago”, and it comes before the time.

**For and since, with the present.** For something that started in the past and **is still going on**, English says “I've lived here for three years”. Spanish uses the **present**, because it's still true:

table: I've lived here for three years.
I've lived here for three years.
I've been here for three years.
I've been studying Spanish for three years.

blocks.p: **{{llevar}}** + an amount of time (+ a gerund) is very common: {{Llevo una hora esperando.}} “I've been waiting for an hour.” It's a regular -ar verb: {{llevas}}, {{lleva}}, {{llevamos}}, {{llevan}}.
**Asking.** {{¿Cuánto tiempo hace que…?}} or {{¿Cuánto tiempo llevas…?}} “How long have you…?”, and {{¿Desde cuándo…?}} “Since when…?”: {{¿Desde cuándo te duele?}} “How long has it been hurting?”

ex.tr: I got married ten years ago.

ex.t: Hace mucho que no te veo.
ex.tr: I haven't seen you in ages.
ex.note: with {{no}}: how long since it last happened

ex.tr: I've worked here since January.
How long have you two been together?

ex.t: Llevo media hora esperando el camión.
ex.tr: I've been waiting for the bus for half an hour.

ex.t: Mi hija nació hace un mes.
ex.tr: My daughter was born a month ago.
How long have you had a fever? — Since last night.

blocks.tip: {{¡Cuánto tiempo!}} or {{¡Hace mucho que no te veo!}} is what you say to someone you haven't seen in a long time.

mistakes.right: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años.
mistakes.tr: I've lived here for three years.
mistakes.why: For something still going on, Spanish says {{desde hace}} (or {{hace … que}}, or {{llevo}}), not {{por}}.
{{hace}} goes before the time.

mistakes.tr: I've been waiting for an hour.
mistakes.why: {{desde}} needs a starting point ({{desde las tres}}). For an amount of time: {{llevo}}, or {{desde hace una hora}}.
