practice.tr: I moved to Chicago five years ago.
I've worked at this company since 2020.

practice.q: “I've been studying Spanish for a year.” Which one?
practice.why: {{llevar}} + time + gerund. ({{Estudio español desde hace un año}} is right too.)

practice.q: At the doctor's. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: How long has your knee been hurting?

options: Me caí hace tres días, cuando corría en el parque.
Me caía hace tres días, cuando corrí en el parque.
lines.why: The event: {{me caí}}; the scene: {{corría}}. And “ago”: {{hace}}.

lines.tr: Let's see, we're going to take a look at it.

practice.tr: I got married ten years ago.

practice.t: Hace dos horas que ___ en la fila.
practice.tr: I've been in line for two hours.
practice.why: {{hace … que}} + the present: it's still going on.

practice.q: Ask a friend “How long have you lived here?”
Your turn: when did you start learning Spanish, and how long have you been at it? Use {{hace}}, and {{llevo}} or {{desde}}.

answers.t: Empecé a estudiar español hace un año. Llevo un año estudiando.
answers.tr: I started learning Spanish a year ago. I've been studying for a year.

answers.t: Estudio español desde enero. Mi primera clase fue hace diez meses.
answers.tr: I've been studying Spanish since January. My first class was ten months ago.

lessons.title: Talk about your experiences
lessons.summary: Ask what someone has done, and say what you have and haven't done: “Have you ever tried chapulines? — No, I've never tried them.”
lessons.topic: the present perfect ({{he ido}}, {{has visto}}); past participles; {{alguna vez}}, {{nunca}}, {{todavía no}}

goal.t: ¿Alguna vez has probado los chapulines? — No, nunca los he probado.
goal.tr: Have you ever tried chapulines (grasshoppers)? — No, I've never tried them.

dialog.t: ¿Has ido a Oaxaca?
dialog.tr: Have you been to Oaxaca?

dialog.t: No, nunca he ido. ¿Tú sí?
dialog.tr: No, I've never been. Have you?

dialog.t: Sí, he ido tres veces. La última vez fui en marzo.
dialog.tr: Yes, I've been three times. The last time I went was in March.

dialog.t: ¿Y has probado el mezcal?
dialog.tr: And have you tried mezcal?

dialog.t: ¡Claro! Y tú lo tienes que probar.
dialog.tr: Of course! And you have to try it.

blocks.p: **What you've done in your life.** For experiences, without saying when, Spanish uses the present perfect, like English “I have…”: {{haber}} + a past participle: {{He ido a Oaxaca.}} “I've been to Oaxaca.”

blocks.means: the form of a verb that goes after “have”: eaten, gone, seen. In Spanish it ends in -ado or -ido: {{hablado}}, {{comido}}.

blocks.p: **Making the participle.** -ar → **-ado** ({{hablar}} → {{hablado}}); -er and -ir → **-ido** ({{comer}} → {{comido}}, {{vivir}} → {{vivido}}). After {{haber}} it never changes. Some common ones are irregular:
**Nothing in between.** {{haber}} and the participle stay together; {{no}} and pronouns go before {{haber}}: {{No lo he visto.}} “I haven't seen it.”

**In Mexico**, the present perfect is mostly for **experiences** (with {{alguna vez}} “ever”, {{nunca}} “never”, {{tres veces}} “three times”) and for what has or hasn't happened **so far** ({{todavía no}} “not yet”, {{últimamente}} “lately”). For something finished, even today, Mexicans use the preterite: {{¿Ya comiste?}} (lesson 29). And as soon as you say when, it's the preterite: {{Fui en marzo.}}

ex.tr: I've never seen snow.
Have you ever been to Guadalajara?
We've traveled a lot this year.

ex.t: Todavía no he terminado el libro.
ex.tr: I haven't finished the book yet.

ex.t: Mi hijo nunca se ha subido a un avión.
ex.tr: My son has never been on a plane.
What have you been up to lately?

ex.t: He escrito tres correos y nadie me ha contestado.
ex.tr: I've written three emails and nobody has answered.

blocks.tip: {{He ido}} and {{he estado}} both mean “I've been (to a place)”: {{¿Has estado en Cancún?}} Answer an experience question, then give the details in the preterite: {{Sí, fui hace dos años.}}

mistakes.why: Pronouns go before {{haber}}, never after it or after the participle.
{{hacer}} has an irregular participle: {{hecho}}.

mistakes.wrong: He ido a Cancún el año pasado.
mistakes.right: Fui a Cancún el año pasado.
mistakes.tr: I went to Cancún last year.
mistakes.why: Once you say when ({{el año pasado}}), use the preterite.

practice.tr: Have you ever had mole?
I've never seen that movie.
Last year I went to Chiapas.
practice.why: A finished time ({{el año pasado}}): the preterite, {{fui}}.

options: Sí, viví en España hace muchos años.
Sí, he vivido en España hace muchos años.

answers.tr: I've traveled to Europe and run a marathon, but I've never seen the Caribbean.

answers.t: He vivido en tres ciudades. Nunca he comido chapulines.
answers.tr: I've lived in three cities. I've never eaten chapulines.

lessons.title: Say why, what for and who for
lessons.summary: Say why you did something, what it's for and who it's for, with the two Spanish “for”s: {{por}} and {{para}}.
lessons.topic: {{por}} or {{para}}; {{¿para qué?}} and {{¿por qué?}}; {{por eso}}

goal.t: Este regalo es para ti. Gracias por todo.
goal.tr: This present is for you. Thanks for everything.

dialog.t: ¿Para quién es el pastel?
dialog.tr: Who's the cake for?

dialog.t: Es para mi mamá. Hoy es su cumpleaños.
dialog.tr: It's for my mom. Today is her birthday.

dialog.t: ¡Qué bonito! ¿Cuánto pagaste por él?
dialog.tr: How lovely! How much did you pay for it?

dialog.t: Quinientos pesos. Lo pedí por internet, para no perder tiempo.
dialog.tr: Five hundred pesos. I ordered it online, so I wouldn't waste time.

dialog.t: ¡Muy bien! Y gracias por invitarme a la fiesta.
dialog.tr: Great! And thanks for inviting me to the party.

blocks.p: **Two words for “for”.** Spanish splits English “for” into {{para}} and {{por}}. A picture that helps: {{para}} looks **ahead**, to a goal, a person who'll receive something, a deadline. {{por}} looks **back** at the cause, or goes **through**: the reason, the exchange, the way.

table: {{por}}: the cause, the exchange, the way
for someone: {{Es para ti.}} It's for you.
because of, thanks for: {{Gracias por la ayuda.}} Thanks for the help.
in order to: {{Estudio para aprender.}} I study to learn.
in exchange for: {{Pagué cien pesos por esto.}} I paid 100 pesos for this.
a deadline: {{Es para el lunes.}} It's due Monday.
through, around: {{Caminamos por el parque.}} We walked through the park.
toward a place: {{Voy para la casa.}} I'm heading home.
by phone, by mail, online: {{por teléfono}}, {{por internet}}
what it's for: {{una taza para café}} a coffee cup
a stretch of time: {{por dos semanas}} for two weeks

blocks.p: **{{para}} + infinitive** = “(in order) to”: {{Ahorro para comprar una casa.}} “I'm saving to buy a house.” **{{por}} + infinitive** = “for doing”, the reason: {{Gracias por venir.}} “Thanks for coming.”
**Two questions.** {{¿Para qué?}} “What for?” asks about the goal; {{¿Por qué?}} “Why?” asks about the cause. And {{por eso}} “that's why” links a reason to what came of it.

ex.t: ¿Para qué estudias español? — Para viajar por Latinoamérica.
ex.tr: What are you studying Spanish for? — To travel around Latin America.
Thanks for everything.

ex.t: Te llamo por teléfono más tarde.
ex.tr: I'll call you later.
The homework is due tomorrow.

ex.t: Cambié mi carro por uno más chico.
ex.tr: I traded my car for a smaller one.

ex.t: Estuve enfermo, por eso no fui.
ex.tr: I was sick, that's why I didn't go.

ex.t: Para mí, la comida de Puebla es la mejor.
ex.tr: For me, Puebla's food is the best.

blocks.tip: Fixed phrases with {{por}}: {{por favor}} (please), {{por fin}} (at last), {{por ejemplo}} (for example), {{por supuesto}} (of course), {{por cierto}} (by the way), {{por ahora}} (for now).

mistakes.why: Thanking for something looks back at the cause: {{por}}.

mistakes.tr: I'm studying to become a doctor.
mistakes.why: In order to, a goal ahead: {{para}}.
The person who'll receive it: {{para}}.

practice.tr: This coffee is for my wife.
Thank you very much for your help.
I'm saving money to buy a car.

practice.q: “I paid 200 pesos for these shoes.” Which one?
practice.why: In exchange for: {{por}}; and a finished payment: {{pagué}}.

options: Porque estaba enferma. Por eso no vine.
Porque estuve enferma. Para eso no vine.

Your turn: why are you learning Spanish? Answer with {{para}} + infinitive, and add a reason with {{porque}}.

lessons.title: Say which one: the person who…, the place where…
lessons.summary: Describe people, places and things in more detail: “The friend who lives in Puebla is coming tomorrow.” “That's what I want.”
lessons.topic: {{que}} (who, which, that), {{donde}} (where), {{lo que}} (what); {{el que}}, {{la que}} (the one who)

goal.t: La amiga que vive en Puebla viene mañana.
goal.tr: The friend who lives in Puebla is coming tomorrow.

dialog.t: ¿Quién es el señor que está al lado de tu papá?
dialog.tr: Who's the man next to your dad?

dialog.t: Es mi tío, el que vive en Tijuana.
dialog.tr: That's my uncle, the one who lives in Tijuana.

dialog.t: ¿Y dónde es esto?
dialog.tr: And where is this?

dialog.t: Es el restaurante donde celebramos el cumpleaños de mi abuela.
dialog.tr: It's the restaurant where we celebrated my grandmother's birthday.

dialog.t: ¡Qué bonito! Lo que más me gusta es el pastel.
dialog.tr: How lovely! What I like best is the cake.

blocks.means: a part of a sentence with its own verb: in “the man who lives here”, the clause is “who lives here”.

blocks.p: **Joining two ideas.** {{Mi amiga vive en Puebla. Mi amiga viene mañana.}} becomes one sentence with {{que}}: {{La amiga que vive en Puebla viene mañana.}} Spanish uses {{que}} for people **and** things, where English says who, which or that.

table: the city where I was born

blocks.p: **Never leave {{que}} out.** English can drop “that”: “the book you lent me”. Spanish can't: {{el libro que me prestaste}}.
**{{donde}}** “where” joins a place: {{el pueblo donde viven mis abuelos}}. In a question it has an accent ({{¿Dónde?}}); joining two ideas, it doesn't.

**{{lo que}}** is “what” in the middle of a sentence, meaning “the thing that”: {{No entiendo lo que dices.}} “I don't understand what you're saying.” {{Lo que necesito es dormir.}} “What I need is sleep.”

**{{el que}}, {{la que}}, {{los que}}, {{las que}}** = “the one(s) who, the one(s) that”, matching the noun you mean: {{¿Cuál quieres? — El que está en la ventana.}} “Which one do you want? — The one in the window.”

ex.t: El señor que vende tamales llega a las siete.
ex.tr: The man who sells tamales comes at seven.
Did you like the movie we saw?

ex.t: Esta es la casa donde crecí.
ex.tr: This is the house where I grew up.
I don't know what I want.

ex.t: Mis amigos que viven en Texas vienen en diciembre.
ex.tr: My friends who live in Texas are coming in December.

ex.t: La chamarra que compré me queda grande.
ex.tr: The jacket I bought is too big for me.

ex.t: Lo que pasa es que no tengo tiempo.
ex.tr: The thing is, I don't have time.

blocks.tip: {{Lo que pasa es que…}} “The thing is…” is the classic Mexican way to start an explanation, or an excuse.

mistakes.wrong: El libro me prestaste es muy bueno.
mistakes.right: El libro que me prestaste es muy bueno.
mistakes.tr: The book you lent me is very good.
mistakes.why: Spanish never leaves out {{que}}.

mistakes.tr: I don't understand what you're saying.
mistakes.why: “What” meaning “the thing that”: {{lo que}}.

mistakes.right: La señora que vive aquí es doctora.
mistakes.tr: The woman who lives here is a doctor.

lessons.title: Tell a friend what to do
lessons.summary: Give instructions, invitations and advice to someone you call {{tú}}: “Come here! Sit down and tell me what happened.”
lessons.topic: {{tú}} commands ({{habla, come, escribe}}); {{ven, ve, haz, pon, di, sal, ten, sé}}; pronouns on the end

goal.t: ¡Ven acá! Siéntate y dime qué pasó.
goal.tr: Come here! Sit down and tell me what happened.

dialog.t: Ayúdame con la salsa, ¿sí?
dialog.tr: Help me with the salsa, will you?

dialog.t: Claro. ¿Qué hago?
dialog.tr: Sure. What do I do?

dialog.t: Corta los tomates y pon la cebolla en la licuadora.
dialog.tr: Cut the tomatoes and put the onion in the blender.

dialog.t: ¿Y luego?
dialog.tr: And then?

dialog.t: Agrega un chile y sal. Y pruébala: dime si está bien.
dialog.tr: Add a chile and some salt. And taste it: tell me if it's okay.

blocks.means: a form of a verb that tells someone to do something: Come! Sit down!

blocks.p: **The friendly command** looks like the “he, she” form of the present: {{habla}} “talk!”, {{come}} “eat!”, {{escribe}} “write!”. Stem changes stay: {{cierra}} (close), {{vuelve}} (come back), {{pide}} (order).
**Eight short ones.** These very common verbs have their own short command:

**Pronouns go on the end**, joined into one word: {{dime}} (tell me), {{ayúdame}} (help me), {{siéntate}} (sit down), {{llámala}} (call her). When that moves the stress back, an accent mark keeps the sound: {{ayuda}} → {{ayúdame}}, {{sienta}} → {{siéntate}}. Short ones don't need it: {{dime}}, {{ponlo}}, {{hazlo}}.
**Softer.** A command isn't rude in Spanish, but you can soften it with {{por favor}}, with {{¿sí?}} at the end, or by asking with the present: {{¿Me ayudas?}} “Will you help me?”

ex.tr: Come and eat!
Pass me the salt, please.
Call me tomorrow.

ex.t: Haz la tarea y luego sal a jugar.
ex.tr: Do your homework and then go out and play.
Be careful.
Tell me the truth.
Put your jacket on, it's cold.

blocks.tip: Mexicans soften commands with {{-le}} on the end: {{¡Ándale!}} (come on!, go on!), {{¡Pásale!}} (come in!), {{¡Córrele!}} (hurry!). You'll hear it everywhere.

mistakes.why: {{venir}} has a short command: {{ven}}.
In a command, the pronoun goes on the end: {{dime}}.

lessons.title: Give directions and instructions
lessons.summary: Give directions and polite instructions to people you call {{usted}}, and to groups: “Go straight for two blocks and turn left.”
lessons.topic: {{usted}} and {{ustedes}} commands ({{siga}}, {{dé vuelta}}, {{pase}}, {{tome}}): the “opposite vowel”

goal.t: Siga derecho dos cuadras y dé vuelta a la izquierda.
goal.tr: Go straight for two blocks and turn left.

blocks.p: **The opposite vowel.** For {{usted}}, the command swaps the vowel of the ending: -ar verbs take **e**, -er and -ir verbs take **a**. Start from the “I” form of the present, drop the -o, and add it:

Because it starts from “I”, the -go verbs and the stem changes come along: {{venga}} (come), {{diga}} (tell), {{ponga}}, {{salga}}, {{cierre}}, {{vuelva}}, {{pida}}. Spelling keeps the sound: {{buscar}} → {{busque}}, {{llegar}} → {{llegue}}, {{cruzar}} → {{cruce}}.

**Five irregulars:** {{ir}} → {{vaya}}, {{ser}} → {{sea}}, {{estar}} → {{esté}}, {{saber}} → {{sepa}}, {{dar}} → {{dé}} (with an accent, to tell it from {{de}} “of”). For a group, add -n: {{vayan}}, {{sean}}, {{den}}. In Mexico, {{ustedes}} commands are for any group, friends included.
**Pronouns go on the end**, as with {{tú}}: {{siéntese}} (sit down), {{dígame}} (tell me; also “How can I help you?”), {{pásenle}} (come in, all of you).

**Directions.** {{siga derecho}} (go straight), {{dé vuelta a la derecha}}, {{dé vuelta a la izquierda}} (turn right, turn left), {{cruce la calle}} (cross the street), {{en la esquina}} (on the corner), {{en el semáforo}} (at the light), {{a dos cuadras}} (two blocks away), {{hasta}} (as far as).

lessons.title: Tell someone not to do something
lessons.summary: Warn, advise and reassure: “Don't worry!” “Don't touch that!” “Don't be late!”
lessons.topic: negative commands ({{no hables}}, {{no se preocupe}}, {{no lo toques}}); pronouns before the verb

goal.t: ¡No te preocupes! Y no llegues tarde.
goal.tr: Don't worry! And don't be late.

dialog.t: Puedes ir a la fiesta, pero no llegues tarde.

blocks.p: **“Don't” uses the opposite vowel.** A negative command, even to {{tú}}, takes the form you learned for {{usted}}, with the {{tú}} ending **-s**: {{no hables}}, {{no comas}}, {{no vengas}}. For {{usted}} and {{ustedes}}, just put {{no}} first: {{no hable}}, {{no hablen}}.

The irregulars come along: {{no vayas}} (don't go), {{no seas}} (don't be), {{no hagas}}, {{no digas}}, {{no pongas}}, {{no salgas}}, {{no estés}}. And the spellings: {{no toques}} ({{tocar}}), {{no llegues}} ({{llegar}}), {{no empieces}} ({{empezar}}).

**Pronouns move to the front.** In “do it”, they go on the end; in “don't do it”, between {{no}} and the verb: {{Tócalo}} → {{No lo toques}}; {{Siéntate}} → {{No te sientes}}; {{Dime}} → {{No me digas}}.

lessons.title: Predict, promise and guess
lessons.summary: Make predictions and promises, and guess about the present: “It'll rain tomorrow.” “I'll call you, I promise.” “Where can Juan be?”
lessons.topic: the simple future ({{hablaré, comerás, vivirá}}; {{tendré, haré, podré, diré, saldré, vendré}}); the future of guessing

goal.t: No te preocupes, te llamaré mañana.

blocks.p: **Two futures.** You already have {{ir a}} + infinitive, the everyday way to talk about plans: {{Voy a viajar en diciembre.}} Spanish also has a one-word future. Mexicans use it less in conversation, but it's everywhere for **predictions**, **promises**, the news and the weather forecast, and for **guessing**.

blocks.means: the tense for what will happen: {{hablaré}} “I'll speak”, {{lloverá}} “it will rain”.

blocks.p: **Easy to make.** Take the whole infinitive and add the endings, the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs. All but “we” carry an accent mark:
**A short list of irregular stems**, with the same endings:
And {{hay}} becomes {{habrá}} “there will be”.

**Guessing.** The future also says what is probably true **right now**: {{¿Dónde estará Juan?}} “Where can Juan be?”, {{Estará en el tráfico.}} “He's probably stuck in traffic.” {{¿Qué hora será?}} “I wonder what time it is.” Mexicans use this a lot.

lessons.title: Say what happens if…
lessons.summary: Talk about real possibilities and what follows: “If it rains, we'll stay home.” “If you have time, call me.”
lessons.topic: {{si}} + present, then the present, {{ir a}}, the future or a command

goal.t: Si llueve mañana, nos quedamos en casa.

blocks.p: **Real possibilities.** {{si}} “if” + the **present**, then the result. Like English, Spanish uses the present after “if” even for the future: {{Si llueve}} “if it rains”, never the future. ({{si}} has no accent; {{sí}} with an accent is “yes”.)

If you have time, call me.
If you study, you'll pass the exam.

blocks.p: **The result** can be the present (very common in Mexico: {{nos quedamos}}), {{ir a}} ({{nos vamos a quedar}}), the future ({{nos quedaremos}}) or a command ({{llámame}}). The two halves can swap places: {{Llámame si tienes tiempo.}}
**Habits and general truths** have the present in both halves: {{Si ceno tarde, no duermo bien.}} “If I eat dinner late, I don't sleep well.”

lessons.title: Say what you want others to do
lessons.summary: Say what you want, need or ask someone else to do: “I want you to come to my party.”
lessons.topic: {{quiero que}}, {{necesito que}}, {{te pido que}} + the present subjunctive

goal.t: Quiero que vengas a mi fiesta.
goal.tr: I want you to come to my party.

dialog.t: Lupita, necesito que me mandes el informe hoy.
dialog.tr: Lupita, I need you to send me the report today.

blocks.p: **One person wants, another does.** When you want to do something **yourself**, use the infinitive: {{Quiero ir.}} “I want to go.” When you want **someone else** to do it, Spanish says “I want that you go”: {{quiero que}} + the other person's verb in the **subjunctive**: {{Quiero que vayas.}} “I want you to go.”

blocks.means: a set of verb forms Spanish uses after words of wanting, wishing, advising and feeling, for what isn't (yet) a fact: {{quiero que vengas}} “I want you to come”.

table: {{Quiero que comas.}} I want you to eat.
{{Necesito que descanses.}} I need you to rest.
{{Prefiero que manejes tú.}} I'd rather you drove.

blocks.p: **You already know the forms.** The present subjunctive is the “opposite vowel” of the {{usted}} commands (lesson 39), with an ending for every person. -ar verbs take **e**, -er and -ir verbs take **a**, starting from the “I” form of the present:

The irregulars are the ones from the commands: {{ir}} → {{vaya}}, {{ser}} → {{sea}}, {{estar}} → {{esté}}, {{saber}} → {{sepa}}, {{dar}} → {{dé}}, and {{haber}} → {{haya}}. Stem changes stay, except for “we”: {{quiera}}, {{pueda}}, {{duerma}}; -ir stem-changers change “we” too: {{durmamos}}, {{pidamos}}.
**The same pattern** follows {{necesito que}} (I need you to), {{te pido que}} (I'm asking you to), {{prefiero que}} (I'd rather you) and {{¿quieres que…?}} (do you want me to…?).

lessons.summary: Wish someone a good day, a good trip or a quick recovery, and say what you hope: “Have a good trip!” “I hope it doesn't rain.”
lessons.topic: {{¡Que…!}} + subjunctive ({{¡Que te vaya bien!}}); {{ojalá (que)}}; {{espero que}}

goal.t: ¡Que te vaya muy bien en tu viaje!
goal.tr: Have a great trip!

dialog.t: ¡Que tengas buen viaje, mi amor!

blocks.p: **{{¡Que…!}} + subjunctive** is how Mexicans wish things to people. It's short for “I want that…”, and you'll hear it every day, at every goodbye:

table: Take care! Have a good day!
a meal, a present, a vacation

blocks.p: To {{usted}}: {{¡Que le vaya bien!}}, {{¡Que tenga buen día!}}, {{¡Que se mejore!}} To a group: {{¡Que les vaya bien!}}

**{{ojalá}} “I hope, if only”** (from Arabic, “if God wills”) is always followed by the subjunctive, with or without {{que}}: {{Ojalá (que) no llueva.}} “I hope it doesn't rain.” On its own, {{¡Ojalá!}} is “I hope so!”.
**{{espero que}} “I hope that”** works like {{quiero que}}: {{Espero que te guste.}} “I hope you like it.” For your own hopes, the infinitive: {{Espero verte pronto.}} “I hope to see you soon.”

practice.q: Say goodbye to your elderly neighbor: “Have a good day!” (to {{usted}})
Your turn: write a short message to a friend who starts a new job tomorrow. Wish them well and say what you hope.

answers.t: ¡Que te vaya muy bien mañana! Espero que te guste el trabajo.
answers.tr: Good luck tomorrow! I hope you like the job.

answers.t: Ojalá que todo salga bien. ¡Que tengas un gran primer día!
answers.tr: I hope everything goes well. Have a great first day!

lessons.title: Give advice and recommendations
lessons.summary: Recommend, advise and say what's important: “I recommend you try the mole.” “It's important that you drink water.”
lessons.topic: {{te recomiendo que}}, {{te aconsejo que}}, {{es mejor que}}, {{es importante que}} + subjunctive; the infinitive for general advice

goal.t: Te recomiendo que pruebes el mole poblano.
goal.tr: I recommend you try the mole poblano.

dialog.t: Voy a ir a la Ciudad de México. ¿Qué me recomiendas?
dialog.tr: I'm going to Mexico City. What do you recommend?

dialog.t: Te recomiendo que vayas a Coyoacán y que visites el Museo Frida Kahlo.
dialog.tr: I recommend you go to Coyoacán and visit the Frida Kahlo Museum.

dialog.t: ¿Es mejor que tome el metro o un taxi?
dialog.tr: Is it better for me to take the subway or a taxi?

dialog.t: El metro es rápido, pero es mejor que no lo tomes en la hora pico.
dialog.tr: The subway is fast, but it's better not to take it at rush hour.

dialog.t: ¿Algo más?
dialog.tr: Anything else?

dialog.t: Sí: es importante que compres los boletos del museo antes. Siempre hay mucha gente.
dialog.tr: Yes: it's important that you buy the museum tickets ahead of time. There are always lots of people.

blocks.p: **Advice for someone** follows the {{quiero que}} pattern: a verb of advising + {{que}} + the subjunctive: {{Te recomiendo que vayas.}} “I recommend that you go.” {{Le aconsejo que descanse.}} “I advise you to rest.”
**“It's … that”.** These phrases take the subjunctive too, because they're about what should happen, not what is:

**With no one in particular** (general advice), use the infinitive: {{Es importante tomar agua.}} “It's important to drink water.” For a person: {{Es importante que tomes agua.}} “It's important that you drink water.”
**Other ways:** {{Deberías}} + infinitive “you should” ({{Deberías descansar}}), and {{Yo que tú…}} “If I were you…” (lesson 48).

ex.t: Te recomiendo que lleves una chamarra.
ex.tr: I recommend you bring a jacket.

ex.t: El doctor me aconseja que camine todos los días.
ex.tr: The doctor advises me to walk every day.
It's better if we leave early.

ex.t: Es importante que los niños duerman bien.
ex.tr: It's important for kids to sleep well.

ex.t: Es necesario que traigas tu pasaporte.
ex.tr: You need to bring your passport.

ex.t: Más vale que no llegues tarde.
ex.tr: You'd better not be late.
It's important to drink lots of water.

blocks.tip: {{¿Qué me recomienda?}} “What do you recommend?” is the perfect question for waiters, taxi drivers and new friends: Mexicans love recommending their favorite places.

mistakes.wrong: Te recomiendo que pruebas el mole.
mistakes.right: Te recomiendo que pruebes el mole.
mistakes.tr: I recommend you try the mole.
mistakes.why: After a verb of advising + {{que}}: the subjunctive, {{pruebes}}.
With no particular person: the infinitive, with no {{que}}.

mistakes.wrong: Es mejor que vamos en metro.
mistakes.right: Es mejor que vayamos en metro.
mistakes.tr: It's better if we go by subway.
mistakes.why: {{es mejor que}} + subjunctive: {{ir}} → {{vayamos}}.

practice.tr: I recommend you leave early.
It's important that you bring your passport.

practice.q: General advice, for everyone: “It's important to sleep eight hours.” Which one?
practice.why: No particular person: the infinitive, without {{que}}.

practice.t: El doctor quiere que ___ menos azúcar.
practice.tr: The doctor wants me to eat less sugar.

practice.q: A friend has a bad back. Give advice. Choose your replies.

options: Te recomiendo que vayas al doctor.
Te recomiendo que vas al doctor.
Es mejor que descanses y no cargues cosas pesadas.
Es mejor que descansas y no cargas cosas pesadas.

practice.tr: It's better if we leave early.

practice.q: Ask a waiter “What do you recommend?” (to {{usted}})
Your turn: a friend is coming to your city. Give them three recommendations with {{te recomiendo que}}, {{es mejor que}} or {{es importante que}}.

answers.t: Te recomiendo que vayas al centro en metro. Es mejor que no manejes, y es importante que pruebes la comida local.
answers.tr: I recommend you take the subway downtown. It's better not to drive, and it's important that you try the local food.

answers.t: Te recomiendo que visites el mercado. Es importante que traigas una chamarra, porque en la noche hace frío.
answers.tr: I recommend you visit the market. It's important to bring a jacket, because it gets cold at night.

lessons.title: Say when something will happen
lessons.summary: Talk about the future with “when”, “as soon as” and “until”: “When you get home, send me a message.” “I'll wait until you come out.”
lessons.topic: {{cuando}} + subjunctive for the future, + the normal forms for habits and the past; {{en cuanto}}, {{hasta que}}, {{antes de que}}

goal.t: Cuando llegues a tu casa, mándame un mensaje.
goal.tr: When you get home, send me a message.

dialog.t: Ya me voy. Es tarde.
dialog.tr: I'm heading out. It's late.

dialog.t: Bueno. Cuando llegues, avísame.
dialog.tr: Okay. Let me know when you get there.

dialog.t: Sí. En cuanto llegue, te mando un mensaje.
dialog.tr: Sure. As soon as I get there, I'll send you a message.

dialog.t: ¿Y cuándo nos vemos otra vez?
dialog.tr: And when will we see each other again?

dialog.t: Cuando regrese de mi viaje. ¡Antes de que te des cuenta!
dialog.tr: When I get back from my trip. Before you know it!

blocks.p: **{{cuando}} has two lives.** For something that **hasn't happened yet**, {{cuando}} takes the **subjunctive**: {{Cuando llegues, llámame.}} “When you get there, call me.” For **habits** and the **past**, which are facts, the normal forms: {{Cuando llego, siempre te llamo}} (a habit), {{Cuando llegué, te llamé}} (the past).

table: When I have money, I'm going to travel.
Whenever I have money, I travel.
When I had money, I traveled.

blocks.p: English uses the present after “when” for the future (“when I **have** money”); Spanish uses the present **subjunctive**. Never the future: not {{cuando tendré}}.

**The same goes for** {{en cuanto}} (as soon as), {{hasta que}} (until) and {{después de que}} (after): {{Te espero hasta que salgas.}} “I'll wait until you come out.” And {{antes de que}} (before) always takes the subjunctive: {{Vámonos antes de que llueva.}} “Let's go before it rains.”
**{{¿Cuándo?}}**, with its accent, asks a question and takes the normal forms: {{¿Cuándo vienes?}} The subjunctive comes only with {{cuando}} joining two ideas.

ex.t: Cuando sea grande, quiero ser astronauta.
ex.tr: When I grow up, I want to be an astronaut.

ex.t: Te llamo en cuanto sepa algo.
ex.tr: I'll call you as soon as I know anything.

ex.t: No me voy hasta que termines.
ex.tr: I'm not leaving until you finish.

ex.t: Cuando vengas a México, te llevo a Teotihuacán.
ex.tr: When you come to Mexico, I'll take you to Teotihuacán.

ex.t: Cuando era niño, me encantaba la lluvia.
ex.tr: When I was a kid, I loved the rain.

ex.t: Lava los platos antes de que lleguen tus papás.
ex.tr: Wash the dishes before your parents get here.

ex.t: Después de que comamos, vamos al parque.
ex.tr: After we eat, we'll go to the park.

blocks.tip: When it's the same person, {{antes de}} and {{después de}} take the infinitive instead: {{Antes de salir, cierra la puerta.}} “Before you leave, close the door.”

mistakes.tr: When you get there, call me.
mistakes.why: {{cuando}} about the future: the subjunctive, never the future.

mistakes.tr: When you get here tomorrow, call me.
mistakes.why: Tomorrow hasn't happened yet: subjunctive, {{llegues}}.
{{antes de que}} always takes the subjunctive.

practice.t: Cuando ___ a casa, mándame un mensaje.
practice.tr: When you get home, send me a message.
When I was a girl, I lived in Monterrey.
practice.why: The past is a fact: the imperfect, {{era}}.

practice.tr: I'll wait for you until you come out.
practice.why: {{hasta que}}, about the future: the subjunctive, {{salgas}}.

practice.q: “Every day, when I get home, I take a shower.” Which one?
options: {{Todos los días, cuando llego a casa, me baño.}}
{{Todos los días, cuando llegue a casa, me baño.}}
{{Todos los días, cuando llegaré a casa, me baño.}}
practice.why: A habit is a fact: the present, {{llego}}.

practice.q: Your sister is leaving on a trip. Choose your replies.

options: ¡Que te vaya bien! Llámame cuando llegues.
¡Que te va bien! Llámame cuando llegas.
lines.why: The wish: {{vaya}}; and {{cuando}} about the future: {{llegues}}.

lines.tr: Sure. Will you pick me up when I get back?

options: Claro, en cuanto me digas la hora.
Claro, en cuanto me dirás la hora.
lines.why: {{en cuanto}}, about the future: the subjunctive, {{digas}}.

practice.tr: I'll call you as soon as I know anything.

practice.q: Your turn: what will you do when you speak Spanish well? Start with {{Cuando hable bien español…}}

answers.t: Cuando hable bien español, voy a viajar por todo México.
answers.tr: When I speak Spanish well, I'm going to travel all over Mexico.

answers.t: Cuando hable bien español, voy a ver películas sin subtítulos y a platicar con mis vecinos.
answers.tr: When I speak Spanish well, I'm going to watch movies without subtitles and chat with my neighbors.

lessons.title: Give your opinion, agree and doubt
lessons.summary: Say what you think, agree or disagree, and say what you doubt: “I think it's a good idea.” “I don't think we have time.”
lessons.topic: {{creo que}} + the normal forms, {{no creo que}} + subjunctive; {{me parece que}}; {{es posible que}}, {{dudo que}}; {{estoy de acuerdo}}

goal.t: Creo que es buena idea, pero no creo que tengamos tiempo.
goal.tr: I think it's a good idea, but I don't think we have time.

dialog.t: ¿Qué te parece si vamos a Guanajuato en Semana Santa?
dialog.tr: How about going to Guanajuato over Easter?

dialog.t: Me parece muy buena idea. Pero creo que va a haber mucha gente.
dialog.tr: I think it's a great idea. But I think there are going to be lots of people.

dialog.t: Sí, es posible que los hoteles estén llenos.
dialog.tr: Yes, the hotels might be full.

dialog.t: No creo que sea tan difícil encontrar algo. Hoy busco.
dialog.tr: I don't think it'll be that hard to find something. I'll look today.

dialog.t: ¡De acuerdo! Vamos.
dialog.tr: Agreed! Let's go.

blocks.p: **What you think: {{creo que}}** “I think (that)” and {{me parece que}} “it seems to me”. The normal forms follow, because you present it as true: {{Creo que tienes razón.}} “I think you're right.” {{Me parece que va a llover.}} Ask with {{¿Qué piensas?}} or {{¿Qué te parece?}} “What do you think?”

**What you doubt: the subjunctive.** When you say you **don't** think something, or you doubt it, or that it's only possible, the subjunctive comes in: {{No creo que tengas razón.}} “I don't think you're right.”

table: {{Creo que es verdad.}} I think it's true.
{{No creo que sea verdad.}} I don't think it's true.
{{Estoy seguro de que viene.}} I'm sure he's coming.
{{Dudo que venga.}} I doubt he's coming.
{{Es verdad que hace calor.}} It's true that it's hot.
{{Es posible que haga calor.}} It might be hot.
{{Me parece que está cerrado.}} I think it's closed.
{{Puede que esté cerrado.}} It may be closed.

blocks.p: **Agreeing and disagreeing.** {{Estoy de acuerdo (contigo).}} “I agree (with you).” {{No estoy de acuerdo.}} “I disagree.” {{Tienes razón.}} “You're right.” {{Creo que sí.}} and {{Creo que no.}} “I think so” and “I don't think so.” {{Depende.}} “It depends.” {{Para mí…}} “For me…”.

ex.t: Creo que este restaurante es el mejor de la ciudad.
ex.tr: I think this restaurant is the best in town.
I don't think it'll rain today.

ex.t: ¿Qué te pareció la película? — Me pareció un poco larga.
ex.tr: What did you think of the movie? — I thought it was a bit long.
We might be late.
I doubt the boss will agree.

ex.t: Estoy de acuerdo contigo: es demasiado caro.
ex.tr: I agree with you: it's too expensive.

ex.t: ¿Tú crees que va a venir? — Creo que no.
ex.tr: Do you think she's coming? — I don't think so.

blocks.tip: {{¿Qué te parece si…?}} + the present is a friendly way to suggest something: {{¿Qué te parece si vamos al cine?}} “How about going to the movies?”

mistakes.why: After {{no creo que}}, the subjunctive: {{sea}}.

mistakes.wrong: Creo que sea una buena idea.
mistakes.right: Creo que es una buena idea.
mistakes.tr: I think it's a good idea.
mistakes.why: {{creo que}} presents it as true: the normal form, {{es}}.
It's {{estar de acuerdo}}, with {{de}} (and never with {{ser}}).

practice.t: No creo que ___ mucho tráfico a esta hora.
practice.tr: I don't think there's much traffic at this time.
I think you're right.
It might rain tomorrow.

practice.q: Choosing a place for dinner. Choose your replies.

lines.t: ¿Qué te parece si vamos al restaurante nuevo?
lines.tr: How about going to the new restaurant?

options: Me parece bien, pero creo que es más caro que el otro.
Me parece bien, pero creo que sea más caro que el otro.
lines.why: {{creo que}}: the normal form, {{es}}; and “than” is {{que}}.

lines.t: Sí, pero dicen que la comida es mejor.
lines.tr: Yes, but they say the food is better.

options: Bueno, dudo que sea mejor, pero vamos.
Bueno, dudo que es mejor, pero vamos.

practice.tr: I don't think it'll rain today.

practice.q: Answer a friend's plan: “I think it's a great idea.”
Your turn: what do you think of learning a language with an app? Give your opinion with {{creo que}}, and a doubt with {{no creo que}} or {{dudo que}}.

answers.t: Creo que es muy útil, pero no creo que sea suficiente: también hay que hablar con la gente.
answers.tr: I think it's very useful, but I don't think it's enough: you also have to talk to people.

answers.t: Me parece una buena idea. Dudo que aprenda todo con una app, pero ayuda mucho.
answers.tr: I think it's a good idea. I doubt I'll learn everything with an app, but it helps a lot.

lessons.title: Say what you would do, and ask politely
lessons.summary: Say what you'd like, what you'd do in someone's place, and ask for things very politely: “I'd love to go.” “Could you help me?”
lessons.topic: the conditional ({{me gustaría, podría, haría}}); {{yo que tú}}; {{quisiera}}; {{deberías}}

goal.t: Me encantaría ir, pero no puedo. ¿Podríamos vernos el domingo?
goal.tr: I'd love to go, but I can't. Could we meet on Sunday?

dialog.t: Buenas tardes. Quisiera una habitación para dos noches.
dialog.tr: Good afternoon. I'd like a room for two nights.

dialog.t: Claro. ¿Le gustaría con vista al mar?
dialog.tr: Of course. Would you like a sea view?

dialog.t: Sí, me encantaría. ¿Cuánto costaría?
dialog.tr: Yes, I'd love that. How much would it be?

dialog.t: Mil ochocientos pesos por noche, con desayuno.
dialog.tr: One thousand eight hundred pesos a night, breakfast included.

dialog.t: Perfecto. ¿Me podría ayudar con las maletas?
dialog.tr: Perfect. Could you help me with my bags?

blocks.p: **Would.** The conditional says what would happen: wishes, polite requests, what you'd do in another situation. It's built like the future (lesson 41), from the whole infinitive with the **same irregular stems**, but with the endings of the -er imperfect:

blocks.means: the verb form for what would happen: {{me gustaría}} “I would like”, {{iría}} “I would go”.

blocks.p: The irregular stems are the future's: {{podría}}, {{haría}}, {{diría}}, {{saldría}}, {{vendría}}, {{pondría}}, {{sabría}}, {{querría}}, and {{habría}} “there would be”.

**Polite requests.** {{¿Podría…?}} “Could you…?” (to {{usted}}), {{¿Podrías…?}} (to {{tú}}), {{¿Le importaría…?}} “Would you mind…?”. To ask for something, {{quisiera}} “I'd like”, a special form of {{querer}}, is the politest of all: {{Quisiera un café.}} And {{me gustaría}} + infinitive is “I'd like to”.

**Advice: {{yo que tú}}.** “If I were you” is simply {{Yo que tú}} + the conditional: {{Yo que tú, no lo compraría.}} “If I were you, I wouldn't buy it.” {{Deberías}} + infinitive is “you should”: {{Deberías descansar.}}

ex.t: Me gustaría aprender a bailar salsa.
ex.tr: I'd like to learn to dance salsa.
Could you speak more slowly, please?

ex.t: Yo que tú, hablaría con el jefe.
ex.tr: If I were you, I'd talk to the boss.
Would you like to have dinner with me on Friday?
I'd like to exchange these shoes.
You should sleep more.

ex.t: Sería genial vivir en la playa.
ex.tr: It would be great to live by the beach.

blocks.tip: {{¿Me podría…?}} is more polite than {{¿Me puede…?}}, which is more polite than {{¿Me das…?}} Choose by the place: at a hotel or a government office, {{¿Me podría…?}}; at a taco stand, {{¿Me da…?}}

mistakes.why: “Would like”: the conditional, {{gustaría}}.
The conditional uses the future's irregular stems: {{podr-}}.

mistakes.wrong: Yo que tú, no lo compro.
mistakes.right: Yo que tú, no lo compraría.
mistakes.tr: If I were you, I wouldn't buy it.
mistakes.why: After {{yo que tú}}, the conditional: {{compraría}}.

practice.tr: I'd like to visit Oaxaca.
Could you close the window, please?
If I were you, I'd talk to her.

practice.q: At a hotel, the most polite way to say “I'd like a room” is…
practice.why: {{quisiera}} is the politest “I'd like”. ({{Quiero}} is fine at a taco stand.)

practice.q: A friend can't decide about a job. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Me ofrecieron un trabajo en Monterrey. ¿Qué harías tú?
lines.tr: They've offered me a job in Monterrey. What would you do?

options: Es importante que lo hables con ellos.
Es importante que lo hablas con ellos.

lines.tr: You're right. I'll tell them today.

practice.tr: Would you like to have dinner with me?

practice.q: Ask very politely: “Could you help me, please?” (to {{usted}})
Your turn: what would you like to do next year? And give a friend some advice with {{yo que tú}}.

answers.t: Me gustaría viajar a Perú. Y tú, yo que tú, aprendería a cocinar.
answers.tr: I'd like to travel to Peru. And you: if I were you, I'd learn to cook.

answers.t: El próximo año me gustaría cambiar de trabajo. Tú deberías tomar vacaciones: yo que tú, iría a la playa.
answers.tr: Next year I'd like to change jobs. You should take a vacation: if I were you, I'd go to the beach.

lessons.title: Imagine: if I had…
lessons.summary: Talk about situations that aren't real, or aren't likely: “If I had more time, I'd learn to play the guitar.” “If I were you…”
lessons.topic: {{si}} + the imperfect subjunctive ({{tuviera, fuera, pudiera}}), then the conditional

goal.t: Si tuviera más tiempo, aprendería a tocar la guitarra.
goal.tr: If I had more time, I'd learn to play the guitar.

dialog.t: ¿Qué harías si ganaras la lotería?
dialog.tr: What would you do if you won the lottery?

dialog.t: Si ganara la lotería, compraría una casa en la playa.
dialog.tr: If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house at the beach.

dialog.t: ¿Y dejarías de trabajar?
dialog.tr: And would you stop working?

dialog.t: ¡Claro! Viajaría por todo el mundo. ¿Y tú?
dialog.tr: Of course! I'd travel all over the world. And you?

dialog.t: Yo le daría la mitad a mi familia y abriría un restaurante.
dialog.tr: I'd give half to my family and open a restaurant.

blocks.p: **Two kinds of “if”.** In lesson 42, {{Si tengo tiempo, te ayudo}} is a real possibility. For something that **isn't real**, or hard to imagine, Spanish uses {{si}} + the **imperfect subjunctive**, then the conditional: {{Si tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría.}} “If I had time, I'd help you” (but I don't).

table: {{Si tengo dinero, viajo.}} If I have money, I'll travel.
{{Si tuviera dinero, viajaría.}} If I had money, I'd travel.
{{Si llueve, no vamos.}} If it rains, we won't go.
{{Si lloviera, no iríamos.}} If it rained, we wouldn't go.
{{Si puedes, ven.}} If you can, come.
{{Si pudieras, ¿vendrías?}} If you could, would you come?

blocks.means: the past form of the subjunctive: {{tuviera}}, {{fuera}}, {{pudiera}}. It follows {{si}} for what isn't real, and it's the form in {{quisiera}}.

blocks.p: **Making it.** Take the “they” form of the **preterite**, drop **-ron**, and add **-ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -ran** (“we” takes an accent on the vowel before). Every irregular preterite comes along:

You already know one: {{quisiera}} “I'd like” is the imperfect subjunctive of {{querer}}. And “if I were you” is {{si yo fuera tú}} (or {{yo que tú}}, lesson 48). Never the conditional right after {{si}}.

ex.tr: If I were rich, I wouldn't work.

ex.t: Si viviera en la playa, nadaría todos los días.
ex.tr: If I lived by the beach, I'd swim every day.
What would you do if you were president?

ex.t: Si yo fuera tú, no le diría nada.
ex.tr: If I were you, I wouldn't tell him anything.

ex.t: Si pudiera, me iría de vacaciones mañana.
ex.tr: If I could, I'd go on vacation tomorrow.

ex.t: Si hablaras con ella, todo sería más fácil.
ex.tr: If you talked to her, everything would be easier.

blocks.tip: In books and songs you'll also meet forms in -se ({{tuviese}}, {{fuese}}). They mean the same; the -ra forms are what Mexicans say.

mistakes.tr: If I had money, I'd travel.
mistakes.why: Right after {{si}}, never the conditional: the imperfect subjunctive, {{tuviera}}.

mistakes.tr: If I had time, I'd help you.
mistakes.why: An imagined “if”: the result is in the conditional, {{ayudaría}}.

mistakes.wrong: Si yo era tú, no iría.
mistakes.right: Si yo fuera tú, no iría.
mistakes.tr: If I were you, I wouldn't go.
mistakes.why: “If I were”: {{si yo fuera}}.

practice.tr: If I had more time, I'd read more.

practice.t: Si fuera millonario, ___ una casa en Cancún.
practice.tr: If I were a millionaire, I'd buy a house in Cancún.

practice.q: Which one is a real possibility (it may well happen)?
practice.why: {{si}} + present: a real possibility. With {{lloviera}}, you're only imagining it.

practice.t: ¿Qué harías si ___ hablar con los animales?
practice.tr: What would you do if you could talk to animals?

practice.q: A fun question at dinner. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Si pudieras vivir en cualquier país, ¿dónde vivirías?
lines.tr: If you could live in any country, where would you live?

options: Porque comería pasta todos los días.
Porque comiera pasta todos los días.

practice.tr: If I were you, I wouldn't tell him anything.

practice.q: Ask a friend “What would you do if you won the lottery?”
Your turn: if you could change one thing in your life, what would it be? Start with {{Si pudiera…}}

answers.t: Si pudiera, viviría en México un año para aprender español.
answers.tr: If I could, I'd live in Mexico for a year to learn Spanish.

answers.t: Si pudiera, trabajaría menos y pasaría más tiempo con mi familia.
answers.tr: If I could, I'd work less and spend more time with my family.

lessons.title: Pass on what someone said
lessons.summary: Tell someone what another person said, asked or wanted: “She said she was tired.” “He asked me to call him.”
lessons.topic: {{dice que}} + present; {{dijo que}} + imperfect; {{me preguntó si}}; {{me pidió que}} + imperfect subjunctive

goal.t: Llamó tu mamá. Dijo que iba a llegar tarde y que la llamaras.
goal.tr: Your mom called. She said she was going to be late and that you should call her.

dialog.t: Oye, llamó Rodrigo.
dialog.tr: Hey, Rodrigo called.

dialog.t: ¿Y qué dijo?
dialog.tr: And what did he say?

dialog.t: Dijo que no podía venir a la fiesta porque estaba enfermo.
dialog.tr: He said he couldn't come to the party because he was sick.

dialog.t: ¡Qué lástima! ¿Algo más?
dialog.tr: What a shame! Anything else?

dialog.t: Sí, preguntó si tenías su libro y te pidió que se lo devolvieras.
dialog.tr: Yes, he asked if you had his book, and he asked you to give it back to him.

blocks.p: **Right now: {{dice que}}.** For what someone is saying now (on the phone, in a message), nothing changes: {{Dice que llega a las ocho.}} “She says she'll be there at eight.” {{Dice que tiene hambre.}}
**In the past: {{dijo que}}.** When you report what someone said earlier, Spanish shifts the verbs back, much as English does:

table: She said she was going to be late.
He said he had already eaten.
He asked me to call him.

blocks.p: {{había}} + participle is “had done”: {{había comido}} “had eaten”. In everyday Mexican speech you'll often just hear the preterite instead: {{Dijo que ya comió.}}

**Questions.** Yes/no questions are reported with {{si}} “if, whether”: {{Me preguntó si tenía hambre.}} “He asked me if I was hungry.” Questions with a question word keep it, accent and all: {{Me preguntó dónde vivía.}} “She asked me where I lived.”

**Requests** are reported with {{que}} + the subjunctive, which in the past is the imperfect subjunctive: {{Me pidió que la llamara.}} “She asked me to call her.” {{Te dijo que no llegaras tarde.}} “She told you not to be late.” So {{decir que}} + the normal forms is “to say that”, and {{decir que}} + subjunctive is “to tell someone to”.
